cards.question: As a private pilot, are you authorized to conduct maintenance on an aircraft?
cards.answer: Yes, a private pilot may conduct maintenance on an aircraft in accordance with Part 43 Appendix A so long as it does not operate under 14 CFR Part 121, 129, or 135.

cards.question: List some examples of tasks a private pilot can legally perform as preventive maintenance.
cards.answer:
The most common and applicable items are noted below with associated list number from Part 43 Appendix A(c).

(1) Removal, installation, and repair of landing gear tires.
(2) Replacing elastic shock absorber cords on landing gear.
(3) Servicing landing gear shock struts by adding oil, air, or both.
(4) Servicing landing gear wheel bearings, such as cleaning and greasing.
(5) Replacing defective safety wiring or cotter keys.
(6) Lubrication not requiring disassembly other than removal of nonstructural items such as cover plates, cowlings, and fairings.
(7) Making simple fabric patches not requiring rib stitching or the removal of structural parts or control surfaces.
(8) Replenishing hydraulic fluid in the hydraulic reservoir.
(10) Applying preservative or protective material to components where no disassembly of any primary structure or operating system is involved and where such coating is not prohibited or is not contrary to good practices.
(11) Repairing upholstery and decorative furnishings of the cabin or cockpit when the repairing does not require disassembly of any primary structure or operating system or interfere with an operating system or affect the primary structure of the aircraft.
(12) Making small simple repairs to fairings, nonstructural cover plates, cowlings, and small patches and reinforcements not changing the contour so as to interfere with proper air flow.
(13) Replacing side windows where that work does not interfere with the structure or any operating system such as controls, electrical equipment, etc.
(14) Replacing safety belts.
(15) Replacing seats or seat parts with replacement parts approved for the aircraft, not involving disassembly of any primary structure or operating system.
(16) Trouble shooting and repairing broken circuits in landing light wiring circuits.
(17) Replacing bulbs, reflectors, and lenses of position and landing lights.
(18) Replacing wheels and skis where no weight and balance computation is involved.
(19) Replacing any cowling not requiring removal of the propeller or disconnection of flight controls.
(20) Replacing or cleaning spark plugs and setting of spark plug gap clearance.
(21) Replacing any hose connection except hydraulic connections.
(22) Replacing prefabricated fuel lines.
(23) Cleaning or replacing fuel and oil strainers or filter elements.
(24) Replacing and servicing batteries.
(25) Cleaning of balloon burner pilot and main nozzles in accordance with the balloon manufacturer's instructions.
(26) Replacement or adjustment of nonstructural standard fasteners incidental to operations.

cards.question: Can a private pilot perform preventive maintenance on an aircraft they do not own or operate?
cards.answer: No, a private pilot must own or operate an aircraft to conduct maintenance on it.

cards.question: What must happen before an aircraft, engine, propeller, or appliance can be approved for return to service after maintenance or alteration?
cards.answer:
No person may approve for return to service any aircraft, airframe, aircraft engine, propeller, or appliance, that has undergone maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, or alteration unless—

(a) The required maintenance record entry has been made;
(b) The repair or alteration form authorized by or furnished by the Administrator has been completed
(c) If a repair or an alteration results in any change in the aircraft operating limitations or flight data contained in the approved aircraft flight manual, those operating limitations or flight data are appropriately revised and set forth

cards.question: What information must be included in a maintenance or preventive maintenance record entry?
cards.answer:
(1) A description of work performed.
(2) The date of completion of the work performed.
(3) The name of the person performing the work if other than the person specified in paragraph (a)(4) of this section.

(4) If the work performed on the aircraft, airframe, aircraft engine, propeller, appliance, or component part has been performed satisfactorily, the signature, certificate number, and kind of certificate held by the person approving the work. The signature constitutes the approval for return to service only for the work performed.

cards.question: Describe Time Before Overhaul (TBO). Is adhering to TBO mandatory?
cards.answer: Time Before Overhaul (TBO) is the time remaining on an aircraft engine until it reaches the manufacturers recommendation for overhaul, or a reconditioning of the power plant. Manufacturer overhaul recommendations, and thus TBO, is technically advisory but highly recommended for Part 91 operations, but mandatory for Part 121 and Part 135 operations.

cards.question: What is a Supplemental Type Certificate?
cards.answer:
A Supplemental Type Certificate (STC) is required when a person alters a product by introducing a major change in type design that does not require an application for a new type certificate under Part 21.19. Some common examples of when an STC would be require include:
➢Engine Upgrades
➢Aerodynamic Modifications (adding winglets, STOL kits)
➢Upgrading standard factory tires to oversized bush wheels

cards.question: What makes an aircraft complex? What must be accomplished before a pilot may act as PIC of a complex aircraft?
cards.answer:
➢ Retractable landing gear
➢ Flaps
➢ Controllable pitch propeller to include aircraft with an engine control system consisting of a digital computer / components controlling the engine and propeller.

No person may act as PIC of a complex aircraft, unless the person has -
(i) received and logged ground and flight training from an authorized instructor in a complex airplane and has been found proficient in the operation and systems of the airplane
(ii) Received a one time endorsement in the pilot's logbook from an authorized instructor

cards.question: What classifies an aircraft as a high-performance airplane? What must be accomplished before a pilot may act as PIC of a high performance airplane?
cards.answer:
An airplane with an engine of more than 200 horsepower

No person may act as PIC of a high-performance airplane unless the person has:
➢ Received and logged ground and flight training from an authorized instructor and been found proficient in the operation and systems of the airplane
➢ Received a one-time endorsement in the pilot's logbook from an authorized instructor who certifies the person is proficient to operate a high-performance airplane.

cards.question: What makes an aircraft a Technically Advanced Airplane?
cards.answer:
An airplane equipped with an electronically advanced avionics system including:
➢ An electronic Primary Flight Display (PFD) that includes: Airspeed Indicator, Turn Coordinator, Attitude Indicator, Heading Indicator, Altimeter, and Vertical Speed Indicator
➢ An electronic Multifunction Display (MFD) that includes a moving map using GPS with the aircraft position displayed
➢ A two axis auto pilot
➢ The PFD and MFD are continuously visible

cards.question: What are the minimum aeronautical experience requirements for a Private Pilot certificate, airplane single-engine land?
cards.answer:
40 hours total flight time, including at least:
➢ 3 hours of cross-country flight training in a single-engine airplane
➢ Except as provided in § 61.110 of this part, 3 hours of night flight training in a single-engine airplane that includes (i) cross-country flight of over 100 nautical miles total distance and (ii) 10 takeoffs and 10 landings to a full stop (with each landing involving a flight in the traffic pattern) at an airport.
➢ 3 hours of flight training in a single-engine airplane on the control and maneuvering of an airplane solely by reference to instruments
➢ 3 hours of flight training with an authorized instructor in a single-engine airplane in preparation for the practical test, which must have been performed within the preceding 2 calendar months from the month of the test
➢ 10 hours of solo flight time in a single-engine airplane, consisting of at least (i) 5 hours of solo cross-country time (ii) One solo cross country flight of 150 nautical miles total distance, with full-stop landings at three points, and one segment of the flight consisting of a straight-line distance of more than 50 nautical miles between the takeoff and landing locations; and (iii) Three takeoffs and three landings to a full stop (with each landing involving a flight in the traffic pattern) at an airport with an operating control tower.

cards.question: What document(s) is a pilot required to have on hand to exercise the privileges of a certificate?
cards.answer:
➢ A pilot certificate issued under Part 61
➢ A photo identification card which must be a driver's license, government ID card, U.S. Armed Forces' ID card, official passport, ID that authorizes unescorted acces to a security ID display area of an airport
➢ A current FAA medical certificate issued under Part 67.

cards.question: What documents is a pilot required to show if a ramp inspection is conducted?
cards.answer:
A pilot is required to present a valid airman certificate (or temporary if applicable), medical certificate (or necessary BasicMed documentation including the Comprehensive Medical Examination Checklist and Medical Education Course Completion certificate), and valid photo identification.

This applies to inspection from:
➢The Administrator (FAA)
➢An authorized representative from the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB)
➢Any Federal, State, or local law enforcement officer
➢An authorized representative from the Transportation Security Administration (TSA)

cards.question: What occurs if a pilot physically misplaces (loses) their pilot certificate?
cards.answer:
A pilot may not exercise the privileges associated with the lost certificate until a temporary or replacement has been obtained.

The pilot may request a temporary certificate and replacement of the certificate via the FAA Airman Certification Branch. The temporary certificate is valid for 60 days from the date of issue.

cards.question: When is a type rating required?
cards.answer:
A type rating is required when:
➢ The maximum certified takeoff weight exceeds 12,500 lbs
➢ Any aircraft powered by a turbojet engine, regardless of weight/size
➢ Any aircraft model designated by the FAA

Note: Pt. 61.31 exact verbiage is "(1) Large Aircraft (except lighter-than-air)." The 12,500 lb figure can be found in Pt. 1 Definitions and Abbreviations and reads "Large aircraft means aircraft of more than 12,500 pounds, maximum certified takeoff weight."

cards.question: When is additional training required for operating pressurized aircraft capable of operating at high altitudes? What does this training include?
cards.answer:
Additional training is required for pressurized aircraft that have a service ceiling or maximum operating altitude, whichever is lower, of 25,000 feet MSL or greater

The training includes:
(i) High-altitude aerodynamics and meteorology
(ii) Respiration
(iii) Effects, symptoms, and causes of hypoxia and any other high-altitude sickness
(iv) Duration of consciousness without supplemental oxygen
(v) Effects of prolonged usage of supplemental oxygen
(vi) Causes and effects of gas expansion and gas bubble formation
(vii) Preventive measures for eliminating gas expansion, gas bubble formation, and high-altitude sickness
(viii) Physical phenomena and incidents of decompression
(ix) Any other physiological aspects of high-altitude flight.

cards.question: Is additional training required to operate a tailwheel aircraft?
cards.answer:
Yes, prior to acting as PIC of a tailwheel aircraft a pilot must receive and log flight training from an authorized instructor in a tailwheel airplane and received the appropriate endorsement. This training must include:
➢ Normal and crosswind takeoffs and landings
➢ Wheel landings
➢ Go around procedures

cards.question: Are pilots required to log all flying time?
cards.answer:
No; pilots must log:
(1) Training and aeronautical experience used to meet the requirements for a certificate, rating, or flight review in accordance with Pt 61.
(2) The aeronautical experience required for meeting recent flight experience requirements of this part.

cards.question: What is required information in logbook entries.
cards.answer:
➢Date
➢ Total flight time
➢ Departing and arriving location (location of simulator)
➢ Type and ID of aircraft, simulator
➢ Type of experience (solo, PIC, SIC)
➢ Conditions of flight (day, night, IMC, simulated IMC)

cards.question: When may a pilot log Pilot in Command (PIC) time?
When is a pilot able to log night time?
cards.answer: Part 1.1 defines night (the applied definition with respect to the logging of night time) as "the time between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight, as published in the Air Almanac, converted to local time."

cards.question: When is a pilot able to log cross country time? Does this differ from the cross country time requirement for Private, Instrument, and Commercial Pilot certifications?
cards.answer: Part 61.1 defines cross-country as any flight that includes a landing at a point other than the point of departure. However, for the purpose of meeting the aeronautical experience requirements for private pilot certificate, commercial pilot certificate, or an instrument rating, the flight must include a point of landing that is at least a straight-line distance of more than 50 NM from the original point of departure.

cards.question: What are the requirements for a Flight Review, and how often must it be completed?
cards.answer:
➢ At least 1 hour of flight training and 1 hour of ground training
➢ Conducted by an authorized instructor
➢ A review of the current general operating and flight rules of Part 91
➢ A review of those maneuvers and procedures that, at the discretion of the person giving the review, are necessary for the pilot to demonstrate the safe exercise of the privileges of the pilot certificate
➢ Completed every 24 calendar months

cards.question: What are the currency requirements to act as PIC of an aircraft?
cards.answer:
➢ Biannual Flight Review within the preceding 24 months.

To carry passengers (day):
➢ Within the preceding 90 days have conducted 3 take offs and 3 landings as the sole manipulator of the flight controls in the same category, class, and type if type rating is required

To carry passengers (night):
➢ Within the preceding 90 days have conducted 3 take offs and 3 landings as the sole manipulator of the flight controls in the same category, class, and type if type rating is required between the time of 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise

cards.question: Give the three different regulatory definitions of "night" used in 14 CFR, and what each governs.
cards.answer:
➢ Part 91.209: Sunset to sunrise - position lights/anti-collision lights must be used
➢ Part 1.1: End of evening civil twilight to beginning of morning civil twilight as published by in the Air Almanac - night flight time may be logged
➢ Part 61.57: 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise - recent flight experience (night currency) requirements to carry passengers AND the requirement for a landing light when carrying passengers for hire

cards.question: What is required of a certificate holder with a permanent change of address?
cards.answer:
Notify the FAA of the change in permanent address within 30 days.

The holder of a pilot, flight instructor, or ground instructor certificate who has made a change in permanent mailing address may not, after 30 days from that date, exercise the privileges of the certificate unless the holder has notified in writing the FAA, Airman Certification Branch, P.O. Box 25082, Oklahoma City, OK 73125, of the new permanent mailing address, or if the permanent mailing address includes a post office box number, then the holder's current residential address.

cards.question: What must a certificate holder do if involved in any Federal or State offense related to the operation of a motor vehicle while intoxicated, impaired, or under the influence of alcohol or drugs.
cards.answer: Submit a written report to the FAA Civil Aviation Security Division not later than 60 days after the motor vehicle accident.

cards.question: What are the eligibility requirements for student pilots (airplane)?
cards.answer:
➢Be at least 16 years of age
➢ Be able to read, speak, write, and understand the English language.

cards.question: What are the limitations of a student pilot?
cards.answer:
A student pilot may not act as PIC of an aircraft:
➢That is carrying a passenger
➢ For compensation or hire
➢ In furtherance of a business
➢ With a flight/surface visibility of less than 3 SM during day or 5 SM during night
➢ When the flight cannot be made with visual reference to the surface
➢ In a manner contrary to any limitations placed in the pilot's logbook by an authorized instructor

cards.question: What are the eligibility requirements for a private pilot certificate?
cards.answer:
(1) Be at least 17 years of age
(2) Be able to read, speak, write, and understand the English language.
(3) Receive a logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor for both the written and practical exams
(4) Pass the required knowledge test on required aeronautical knowledge areas
(5) Meet the aeronautical experience requirements
(6) Pass the practical test
(7) Hold either a student pilot certificate or sport pilot certificate.

cards.question: What are the limitations of a Private Pilots Certificate?
cards.answer: Cannot act as Pilot in Command of an aircraft that is carrying passengers or property for compensation or hire

cards.question: May the holder of a Private Pilot Certificate share the cost of an aircraft rental? If so, what requirement must exist for the sharing not to be considered compensation?
cards.answer:
Yes, Private Pilots may split operating costs including fuel, oil, airport expenditures and rental fees so long as the pilot pays his/her pro rata share. The pilot accepting any additional compensation is not legal. Additionally, private pilots are not permitted to "hold out" a willingness to transport persons or property for sharing costs.

The FAA has consistently interpreted Part 61.113 to mean that a private pilot must have a common purpose with passengers and have a personal reason for traveling to the destination.

cards.question: Describe the different medical certificates, how long they are good for, and the privileges associated with each.
cards.answer:
First Class:
➢ Over 40: Valid for 6 months, then 2d Class for 6 months, then 3d class for 12 months
➢ Under 40: Valid for 12 months, then 3d Class for 48 months
➢ Privileges: ATP, CPL privileges

Second Class:
➢ Valid for 12 months regardless of age
➢ Over 40: After 12 months 3d Class valid for remaining 12 months
➢ Under 40: 3d Class valid for remaining 48 months
➢ Privileges: Can exercise CPL privileges

Third Class:
➢ Over 40: Valid for 24 months
➢ Under 40: Valid for 60 months
➢ Privileges: Can exercises PPL privileges

cards.question: What is a pilot's obligation if a new medical condition develops or new medication is taken?
cards.answer:
A pilot has the obligation to not act as PIC or crewmember of an aircraft if a new medical condition develops or new medication is taken that would prevent them from meeting the requirements for the medical certificate. A pilot should contact an Aviation Medical Examiner (AME) if there is ever any uncertainty.

Exact Part 61.53 verbiage: No person who holds a medical certificate may act as PIC, or in any other capacity as a required flight crewmember, while that person:
(1) Knows or has reason to know of any medical condition that would make the person unable to meet the requirements for the medical certificate necessary for the pilot operation; or
(2) Is taking medication or receiving other treatment for a medical condition that results in the person being unable to meet the requirements for the medical certificate necessary for the pilot operation.

cards.question: What does Part 68 govern?
cards.answer: Part 68 outlines the education and examination requirements for operating an aircraft without holding a medical certificate. The BasicMed requirements.

cards.question: What are the BasicMed requirements and at what intervals?
cards.answer:
➢ Previously held FAA medical certificate issued after July 15, 2006
➢ Comprehensive Medical Examination Checklist completed every 48 months
➢ Online course completed every 24 months
➢ Course Completion Certificate and medical checklist must be provided if requested by an inspector

cards.question: What are the aircraft and operating limitations for flying under BasicMed?
cards.answer:
The following limitations apply to individuals flying under BasicMed:
➢ Maximum certified T/O Weight - 12,500 lbs
➢ Maximum of 7 total occupants
➢ At or below 18,000 ft MSL
➢ Not to exceed 250 kts
➢ Cannot fly for compensation or hire
➢ NOTE: These limitations apply to both the PIC and any crew.

cards.question: Can a pilot use BasicMed if their most recent FAA medical certificate was denied, suspended, or revoked?
cards.answer:
No, if a pilot's most recent FAA medical certificate was denied, suspended, or revoked, you cannot use BasicMed.

If in the past a medical certificate was denied, suspended, or revoked and you subsequently received an FAA medical certificate you may be eligible for BasicMed.

cards.question: What is the pilot in command's responsibility and authority?
cards.answer: The PIC of an aircraft is directly responsible for, and is the final authority as to, the operation of that aircraft. If an in-flight emergency occurs, the PIC may deviate from any rule of of Part 91 to meet that emergency.

cards.question: Who is responsible for determining that an aircraft is in airworthy condition, and what must the pilot in command do if it becomes unairworthy during flight?
cards.answer:
(a) No person may operate a civil aircraft unless it is in an airworthy condition.
(b) The pilot in command of a civil aircraft is responsible for determining whether that aircraft is in condition for safe flight. The pilot in command shall discontinue the flight when unairworthy mechanical, electrical, or structural conditions occur.

cards.question: What is the definition of "airworthy," and who ultimately determines airworthiness before each flight?
cards.answer: An aircraft is airworthy when it conforms to its type certificate/approved data and is in a condition for safe operation. While maintenance personnel certify work performed, the pilot in command makes the final determination that the aircraft is in a condition safe for the intended flight prior to each flight.

cards.question: Can objects be dropped from aircraft?
cards.answer:
Yes, so long as reasonable precautions are taken to avoid injury or damage to persons or property.

"No pilot in command of a civil aircraft may allow any object to be dropped from that aircraft in flight that creates a hazard to persons or property. However, this section does not prohibit the dropping of any object if reasonable precautions are taken to avoid injury or damage to persons or property."

cards.question: What are the FAA's rules on alcohol and drug use?
cards.answer:
No person may act or attempt to act as a crewmember of a civil aircraft—
(1) Within 8 hours after the consumption of any alcoholic beverage (8 hours bottle to throttle)
(2) While under the influence of alcohol
(3) While using any drug that affects the person's faculties in any way contrary to safety
(4) While having an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater in a blood or breath specimen. Alcohol concentration means grams of alcohol per deciliter of blood or grams of alcohol per 210 liters of breath.

cards.question: What guidance should a pilot follow regarding taking medications (prescription or over-the-counter) before flying?
cards.answer: A pilot should not fly while taking any medication that affects the faculties in a way contrary to safety (per 91.17), should know the side effects of any medication taken, and should wait an appropriate period after starting a new medication or consult an Aviation Medical Examiner (AME) if uncertain about a medication's effects or FAA acceptability.

cards.question: What protection does the Aviation Safety Reporting Program (the "NASA form") provide, and what are its limits?
cards.answer: The FAA will not use reports submitted to the National Aeronautics and Space Administrator under the Aviation Safety Reporting Program in any enforcement action except information concerning accidents or criminal offenses.

cards.question: What information must the PIC of an aircraft become familiar with prior to each flight?
cards.answer:
The PIC will become familiar with the following (acronym NWKRAFT):
➢ NOTAMs
➢ Weather reports and forecasts
➢ Known ATC delays
➢ Runway Lengths
➢ Alternates Available - should flight plan not be able to be completed
➢ Fuel Requirements
➢ Takeoff and Landing Distance

cards.question: What are the requirements for flight crewmembers to remain at their duty stations?
cards.answer:
Each crewmember will be at their station unless the absence is necessary to perform duties pertaining to the operation of the aircraft or physiological needs and will:
➢ Keep their safety belt fastened while at the crewmember station
➢ Keep his/her shoulder harness fastened during taxi, takeoff, and landing

cards.question: What are the rules for operating an aircraft near other aircraft, including formation flight?
cards.answer:
➢ No person may operate an aircraft so close to another aircraft as to create a collision hazard
➢ No person may operate an aircraft in formation flight unless by arrangement by the PIC of both aircraft
➢ No person carrying passengers for hire may fly in formation flight

cards.question: Explain the right-of-way rules. Explain head on collision avoidance and overtaking situations.
cards.answer:
➢ An aircraft in distress has right-of-way over all other air traffic
➢ Converging (same category) - aircraft to the other's right has the right of way
➢ A balloon has the right-of-way over any other category
➢ An aircraft towing or refueling other aircraft has the right away over all other powered aircraft
➢ An airship has the right-of-way over all other powered aircraft, except for an aircraft towing or refueling another
➢ While approaching head on, each aircraft shall alter course to the right
➢ An overtaking aircraft shall overtake on the right
➢ During approach/landing, the lower aircraft has the right away

cards.question: What are the aircraft speed restrictions below 10,000 feet MSL, and near/within an airspace class where a speed limit applies?
cards.answer:
➢ Below 10,000' MSL, indicated airspeed will not exceed more than 250 kts
➢ Within 4NM of Class C and Class D airspace and below 2,500 AGL, indicated airspeed will not exceed more than 200 kts
➢ Within a VFR corridor or airspace underlying a Class B airspace, indicated airspeed will not exceed more than 200 kts

cards.question: What are the minimum safe altitudes over congested areas, over other-than-congested areas, and everywhere else?
cards.answer:
Anywhere - An altitude allowing, if a power unit fails, an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons/property

Over Congested Areas - 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal radius of 2,000 feet

Other than Congested Areas - 500 feet above the surface, except over open water or sparsely populated areas, 500 feet from any vessel vehicle, or structure

cards.question: What are a pilot's obligations regarding ATC clearances and instructions? Can a pilot ever deviate?
cards.answer: No PIC may deviate from an ATC clearance unless an amended clearance is obtained, an emergency exists, or the deviation is in response to a traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory.

cards.question: What are Land and Hold Short Operations (LAHSO), and what is a pilot's responsibility?
cards.answer:
LAHSO is an air traffic control procedure that requires pilot participation to balance the needs for increased airport capacity and system efficiency by simultaneous use of two intersecting runways, consistent with safety. If LAHSO are accepted by the pilot, the pilot must stop short or exit the runway of use prior to a different intersecting and active runway. ATC may issue LAHSO and pilots may accept if the PIC determines that the aircraft can safely land and stop within the Available Landing Distance (ALD). The PIC has the final authority to accept or decline any land and hold short clearance.

The below image is an example of a possible LAHSO scenario. Note the  Runway Holding Position Signs and Hold Short Marking for Rwy 13 - 31

cards.question: How is a closed runway marked, and what should a pilot do?
cards.answer: A closed runway is marked with a yellow "X" at each end (and sometimes at intervals along the runway). A pilot should not land, take off, or taxi on a closed runway.

cards.question: What is the standard pattern turn direction at uncontrolled airports?
cards.answer: The standard pattern turn direction is left at uncontrolled airports. Right hand pattern airports / runways can be found in the Chart Supplement or when looking at an airport's information block on a VFR Sectional, where RP indicated Right Pattern and RP # indicated Right Pattern for a specific runway(s).

cards.question: What is the standard traffic pattern altitude, and how should a pilot enter the pattern at a non-towered airport?
cards.answer: Standard traffic pattern altitude is typically 1,000 ft AGL but can vary by airport; pilots should check the Chart Supplement for each airport. The recommended entry is a 45-degree angle to the downwind leg, at pattern altitude, entering at midfield.

cards.question: What are the communication requirements at a towered airport in any airspace?
cards.answer: Positive 2 way communication with the tower must be established to operate to, from, through, or at a towered airport. If operating near a larger airport with an approach frequency, communicate with approach to include position, altitude, direction of travel, and request.

cards.question: What are the requirements to operate in Class D airspace?
cards.answer: Establish positive two way communication with the controlling ATC facility.

cards.question: What are the requirements to operate in Class C airspace?
cards.answer:
➢ Establish positive two way communication with ATC facility
➢ Mode C Transponder
➢ ADSB-Out

cards.question: What equipment and clearance is required to operate in Class B airspace?
cards.answer:
➢ Explicit ATC clearance required from the controlling agency obtained via 2-way radio
➢ Mode C Transponder
➢ ADS-B Out

NOTE: The equipment noted above is also mandated in the Mode C Veil, a 30 NM radius around major airports

cards.question: What are the different types of Special Use Airspace?
cards.answer:
Acronym MCPRAWN:
➢ M - MOA, Military Operations Area. Heavy military training, acrobatic flight, high speed maneuvers
➢ C - CFA, Controlled Firing Area. Ground activities that stop immediately if an aircraft approaches, not charted
➢ P - Prohibited Area. Flight is completely forbidden due to national security or welfare purposes
➢ R - Restricted Area. Contain invisible hazards; can be flown through if inactive (ask ATC)
➢ A - Alert Area. Zones with a high volume of pilot training or unusual aerial activity
➢ W - Warning Area. Hazardous military activity zones located over domestic or international waters
➢ N - NSA, National Security Area. Airspace with increased security and pilot ground tracking requests

cards.question: What is a Temporary Flight Restriction (TFR), and how can a pilot check for active TFRs before a flight?
cards.answer: A TFR is a regulatory action restricting flight in a defined area, often issued for VIP movement, disasters/firefighting, space launches, major sporting events, or security reasons. Pilots can check for active TFRs via a standard weather briefing, the FAA TFR website, NOTAMs, or graphical user interfaces on most EFBs.

cards.question: What clearance is required to operate in Class A airspace, and why does this generally not apply to a VFR-only private pilot?
cards.answer: An IFR clearance is required to operate in Class A airspace. Most VFR-only private pilots will not be conducting IFR.

cards.question: What is CTAF, and how is it used at a non-towered airport?
cards.answer:
The Common Traffic Advisory Frequency (CTAF) is a designated advisory frequency (UNICOM, MULTICOM, or dedicated frequency) used by pilots to self-announce position and intentions when operating in and around an airport without an operating control tower.

Uses include taxi announcements, announcing position / altitude / direction of travel when near a non-towered airport, traffic pattern advisories including calls for entering each pattern leg, and announcing intentions.

cards.question: Under what conditions can passengers be carried for a charitable, nonprofit, or community event, and how is this different from normal compensation rules?
cards.answer:
➢ Flight is non-stop, ends at the same airport, and does not exceed 25-statute miles from airport.
➢ Aircraft has maximum of 30 seats, excluding crewmember seats
➢ Aircraft maximum payload capacity of 7,500 lbs
➢ No acrobatic or formation flight
➢ Compensation for the flight does not exceed the pro rata share
➢ This can be done without a CPL

cards.question: What are the minimum fuel requirements for a VFR flight during the day? At night?
cards.answer:
No person may begin a flight in an airplane under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed—
(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes
(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.

cards.question: What are the basic VFR weather minimums (visibility and cloud clearance) required in Class A airspace?
cards.answer: Not Applicable, IFR clearance required

cards.question: What are the basic VFR weather minimums (visibility and cloud clearance) required in Class B airspace?
cards.answer:
➢Visibility: 3 SM
➢Cloud Clearance: Clear of Clouds

cards.question: What are the basic VFR weather minimums (visibility and cloud clearance) in Class C airspace?
cards.answer:
➢Visibility: 3 SM
➢Cloud Clearance: 1,000 ft above, 500 ft below, 2,000 ft horizontal

cards.question: What are the basic VFR weather minimums (visibility and cloud clearance) in Class D airspace?
cards.answer:
➢Visibility: 3 SM
➢Cloud Clearance: 1,000 ft above, 500 ft below, 2,000 ft horizontal

cards.question: What are the basic VFR weather minimums (visibility and cloud clearance) in Class E airspace??
cards.answer:
Less than 10,000 ft MSL:
➢Visibility: 3 SM
➢Cloud Clearance: 1,000 ft above, 500 ft below, 2,000 ft horizontal

At or above 10,000 ft:
➢Visibility: 5 SM
➢Cloud Clearance: 1,000 ft above, 1,000 ft below, 1 SM horizontal

cards.question: What are the basic VFR weather minimums (visibility and cloud clearance) for Class G airspace?
cards.answer:
1,200 ft or less AGL regardless of MSL, Day:
➢Visibility: 1 SM
➢Cloud Clearance: Clear of clouds

1,200 ft or less AGL regardless of MSL, Night:
➢Visibility: 3 SM
➢Cloud Clearance: 1,000 ft above, 500 ft below, 2,000 ft horizontal

More than 1,200 ft AGL AND at/above 10,000 ft MSL:
➢Visibility: 5 SM
➢Cloud Clearance: 1,000 ft above, 1,000 ft below, 1 SM horizontal

cards.question: What is Special VFR, what are its weather minimums, and what is required to operate under it at night?
cards.answer:
Special VFR allows a pilot to operate an aircraft in controlled airspace when meteorological conditions do not satisfy VFR minimums.
➢ Limited to the upward extension of lateral boundaries of Class B, C, D, E and below 10,000 ft MSL
➢ Special VFR must specifically be requested by the pilot, ATC cannot initiate it
➢ Day - Special VFR requires the pilot to hold at least a private pilot certificate or higher, 1 SM flight visibility, and 1 SM ground visibility
➢ Night - Special VFR requires that the pilot and aircraft BOTH must be IFR capable

cards.question: What visibilities and ceilings are associated with VFR, MVFR, IFR, and LIFR?
cards.answer:
LIFR (Low IFR). Ceiling less than 500 feet and/or visibility less than 1 mile.
➢IFR. Ceiling 500 to less than 1,000 feet and/or visibility 1 to less than 3 miles.
➢MVFR (Marginal VFR). Ceiling 1,000 to 3,000 feet and/or visibility 3 to 5 miles inclusive.
➢VFR - Ceiling greater than 3,000 feet and visibility greater than 5 miles; includes sky clear.

cards.question: Explain the VFR cruising altitude rule and how you'd apply it based on your magnetic course.
cards.answer:
VFR cruising altitude standards begin when an aircraft is operating above 3,000 ft AGL and unless authorized by ATC are as follows:
➢ On a magnetic course of 0-179 degrees magnetic: odd thousand ft MSL + 500 (3,500 feet, 5,500 feet, 7,500 feet)

➢ On a magnetic course of 180-359 degrees magnetic: even thousand ft MSL + 500 (4,500, 6,500, 7,500)

cards.question: What prerequisite is needed to fly VFR within 60 NM of the Washington, DC VOR/DME (the "DC SFRA")?
cards.answer:
The pilot must have completed the FAA DC SFRA Special Awareness Training (FAA Safety Course ALC-405). Of note, upon completion of this training there are multiple reference sheets and smart pack PDFs that can be downloaded and saved into an EFB, onto a device, or printed for future flights into the DC SFRA. Additionally, although the course is a one time requirement, it is recommended a pilot completes reviews the course if significant time has passed since completion and the upcoming flight into the DC SFRA. 

https://www.faasafety.gov/gslac/ALC/courseLanding.aspx?cID=405

cards.question: What documentation must be on board an aircraft during flight? How long are these items valid for?
cards.answer:
Acronym SPARROW:
➢ S - Supplements
➢ P - Placards
➢ A - Airworthiness Certificate, valid so long as the aircraft is kept in an airworthy state
➢ R - Registration, valid for 7 years (expires on the last day of the month of issue)
➢ R - Radio Station License, only required for international flights
➢ O - Operating Limitations (POH)
➢ W - Weight and balance

cards.question: Where would a pilot find a list of placards required for an aircraft?
cards.answer: A list of required placards can be found in the Limitations section of an AFM/POH.

cards.question: Describe supplements and name some examples of AFM supplements?
cards.answer:
Supplements contains information necessary to safely and efficiently operate the aircraft when equipped with optional systems and equipment not provided with the standard aircraft. The appropriate information is inserted into the flight manual at the time of installation. Some examples include:
➢Autopilots
➢Navigation Systems (GPS)
➢Avionic Upgrades

cards.question: What instruments and equipment are required for day VFR flight?
cards.answer:
Acronym A TOMATO FLAMES:
➢ Airspeed Indicator
➢ Tachometer
➢ Oil Pressure Gauge
➢ Manifold Pressure Gauge (altitude engine)
➢ Altimeter
➢ Temperature Gauge (liquid cooled cooled)
➢ Oil Temperature Gauge (air cooled engine)
➢ Fuel Gauge
➢ Landing Gear Position Indicator
➢ Anti-collision Lights
➢ Magnetic Compass
➢ ELT
➢ Seat Belts

cards.question: What additional equipment is required for night VFR flight beyond the day list?
cards.answer:
Acronym FLAPS:
➢ Fuses (one spare set accessible to pilot)
➢ Landing Light (if aircraft operated for hire)
➢ Anti-collision Lights
➢ Position Lights
➢ Source of Power

cards.question: What aircraft lighting is required from sunset to sunrise?
cards.answer: Navigation (Position) Lights.

cards.question: What are the aircraft position (navigation) light colors?
cards.answer:
➢ Steady Red - Left (port) wingtip
➢ Steady Green - Right (starboard) wingtip
➢ Steady White - Tail

This allows another pilot to determine an aircraft's direction of travel at night

cards.question: When is supplemental oxygen required for the flight crew, and when for passengers?
cards.answer:
➢ Cabin pressure altitudes above 12,500 ft MSL up to and including 14,000 ft MSL: the required minimum flight crew must be provided with and use supplemental oxygen for any part of the flight at those altitudes lasting more than 30 minutes.

➢ Above 14,000 ft MSL: the required minimum flight crew must be provided with and use supplemental oxygen the entire time at those altitudes.

➢ Above 15,000 ft MSL: each occupant must be provided with supplemental oxygen (passengers are not required to use it).

Pressurized aircraft:
➢ Above FL 250: at least a 10-minute supply of supplemental oxygen must be available for each occupant, in addition to the above, in case a descent is needed after loss of pressurization.
➢ Above FL 350: one pilot at the controls must wear and use a sealed oxygen mask (exception up to FL 410 when two pilots are at the controls, each with a quick-donning mask that can be put on within 5 seconds).

cards.question: What must be done to legally fly an aircraft with inoperative instruments or equipment when there's no Minimum Equipment List (MEL)?
cards.answer:
Is the piece of equipment:
➢ Required under 91.205? -> cannot fly
➢ Indicated as required as part of the VFR-day type certificate and KOEL -> cannot fly
➢ Required by an AD -> cannot fly

THEN:
➢ Remove the equipment (if necessary) or fuze (deactivated)
➢ Placard cockpit control as "Inoperative"
➢ Record in accordance with Pt 43

cards.question: Where is a transponder required to operate an aircraft?
cards.answer:
An operable transponder with Mode C (altitude reporting) is required:
➢ In Class A, B, and C airspace
➢ In all airspace within 30 NM of a Class B primary airport (Mode C veil), from the surface up to 10,000 ft MSL
➢ Above 10,000 ft MSL in the 48 contiguous states (excluding at/below 2,500 ft AGL)
➢ Above the ceiling and within the lateral boundaries of a Class B or Class C airspace area designated for an airport upward to 10,000 ft MSL.

cards.question: Where is ADS-B Out equipment required, and what's its purpose?
cards.answer:
➢ Class A, Class B (to include Mode C veil), Class C airspace at all altitudes
➢ Class E airspace above 10,000 ft MSL (excluding at / below 2,500 ft AGL)
➢ Above Class B and Class C Airspace
➢ Class E airspace at and above 3,000 ft MSL over the Gulf of Mexico within 12 NM of the US coastline

cards.question: Under what conditions is aerobatic flight prohibited?
cards.answer:
Aerobatic flight is prohibited:
➢ Over any congested area of a city, town, settlement
➢ Over an open air assembly of persons
➢ Within the lateral boundaries of the surface areas of Class B, Class C, Class D, Class E airspace designated for an airport
➢ Within 4 NM of the center line of any Federal airway
➢ Below 1,500 ft above the surface
➢ When flight visibility is less than 3 SM

cards.question: What must happen before an aircraft can be flown again after maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, or alteration? What additional considerations exist for the carrying of passengers
cards.answer:
(1) It must be approved for return to service by a person authorized under Part 43.7
(2) The maintenance record entry required by Part 43.9 or 43.11 must be made
(3) Prior to the carrying of passengers after an aircraft has been maintained, rebuilt, or altered in a way that may have appreciably changed its flight characteristics or substantially affected its operation in flight until an appropriately rated pilot with at least a private pilot certificate flies the aircraft, makes an operation check of the maintenance / alteration performed, and logs the flight in the aircraft records.

cards.question: What inspections do GA aircraft require and at what intervals?
cards.answer:
Acronym AV1ATES:
➢ Annual - completed yearly
➢ VOR Check - every 30 days for flights under IFR
➢ 100 Hour Inspection - every 100 hours of flight time for aircraft used to carry passenger for hire or flight instruction (+10 hours to fly to inspection, time is deducted from next 100 hours)
➢ Airworthiness Directives - Per specific schedules
➢ Transponder - Every 24 months
➢ Emergency Landing Transmitter (ELT) - Every 12 calendar months or after 50% battery life used
➢ Static System / Altimeter - Test every 24 months

cards.question: If an aircraft has passed its annual inspection date can it legally be flown to an inspection location? If so, are there any additional requirements?
cards.answer: An aircraft that has passed its required annual inspection date cannot legally be flown to an inspection location unless a special flight permit has been issued for the flight. The special flight permit will include limitations to the flight that may include restrictions such as VFR Day Only and Essential Flight Crew Only. A special flight permit may be obtained by calling the local Flight Safety District Office (FSDO).

cards.question: Can an aircraft be legally flown if it has passed its 100 hour inspection requirement?
cards.answer:
Yes, the aircraft can be flown for up to 10 hours if necessary to reach a location where the inspection can be performed. These 10 hours are subtracted from the start of the next 100 hour interval.

For example, if an aircraft is due for a 100 hour inspection at 100.0 hours, and it takes 5.0 hours (bringing time to 105.0) to arrive at the inspection location, the next inspection is due at 200.0 hours.

cards.question: What is a special flight permit, when are they generally issued, and how does a pilot obtain one?
cards.answer:
A special flight permit may be issued for an aircraft that may not currently meet applicable airworthiness requirements (such as being out of annual inspection) but is capable of safe flight, for the following purposes:
(1) Flying the aircraft to a base where repairs, alterations, or maintenance are to be performed, or to a point of storage.
(2) Delivering or exporting the aircraft.
(3) Production flight testing new production aircraft.
(4) Evacuating aircraft from areas of impending danger.
(5) Conducting customer demonstration flights in new production aircraft that have satisfactorily completed production flight tests.

Special flight permits may be obtained by calling a local FSDO.

cards.question: What happens to an aircraft's maintenance records when it's sold?
cards.answer: All maintenance records are transferred to the new owner upon purchase.

cards.question: What is an Advisory Circular, and what authority does it carry compared to a regulation?
cards.answer:
Advisory Circular's (ACs) are guidance documents that the FAA uses to distribute information to the aviation community. They are information only and not regulatory in nature. Some example ACs include
➢ AC 90-66 Non-Towered Airport Operations
➢ AC 91-92 Pilot's Guide to a Preflight Briefing
➢ AC 60-22 Aeronautical Decision Making
➢ AC 91-74 Pilot Guide: Flight in Icing Conditions

cards.question: What are the different types of NOTAMs and what is their purpose?
cards.answer:
NOTAM (D) - Widespread aviation alert providing essential, real-time information about the National Airspace System including runway closures, NAVAIDs, and airport hazards.

FDC NOTAM - issued by the National Flight Data Center and contain information that is regulatory in nature including, but not limited to, changes to charts, procedures, and airspace usage.

Pointer NOTAM - issued to highlight or draw attention to another NOTAM.

Military NOTAM - pertain to military airfields, defense exercises, and special activity airspace

UAS Operating Area NOTAM - issued to alert airspace users about a UAS being operated. In general, a UAS NOTAM is not required for UAS operating as follows:
➢At or below 400 ft AGL, in Class G airspace, or at / below the establish UAS facility map altitudes in Class B, C, D, E surface areas
➢UAS weighs less than 55 lbs
➢UAS remains within visual line of site➢UAS has a maximum airspeed of 100 mph (87 kts) or less

cards.question: What do Category, Class, and Type mean with respect to aircraft?
cards.answer:
Category - A broad classification of aircraft (airplane, rotorcraft, glider)

Class - Classification of aircraft within a category with similar operating characteristics (ASEL, ASES, AMEL, AMES)

Type - A specific make and basic model of aircraft (Cessna 172, PA-28)

cards.question: What is the PAVE checklist, and what does each letter stand for?
cards.answer:
A preflight checklist used to assess risk before a flight:
➢ Pilot in Command (PIC) - Am I ready for this trip in terms of experience, recency, currency, documents. Use of the IMSAFE checklist
➢ Aircraft - Is this the right aircraft for the flight? Am I familiar with the aircraft? Is it equipped properly? Can the aircraft carry the planned load? Can the aircraft perform as intended at the altitudes intended?
➢ enVironment - Weather, terrain, airspace, time of day
➢ External Pressures - People's schedules, a passenger the pilot does not want to disappoint, desire to impress someone, pilot's goal-completion orientation

cards.question: What is the IMSAFE checklist?
cards.answer:
A checklist used by a PIC to self assess physical and mental readiness for flying:
➢ Illness - Am I sick?
➢ Medication - Am I taking medications that could effect my performance?
➢ Stress - Am I under any stress including money, job, relationships?
➢ Alcohol - When was the last time I drank? Can I legally fly? Is it still affecting me?
➢ Fatigue - Am I tired? Did I get adequate rest?
➢ Emotion - Am I emotionally upset?

cards.question: Describe the SAFETY acronym for briefing passengers?
cards.answer:
The SAFETY acronym is a method for briefing passengers before a flight developed by the FAA as part of its FAA Safety Team (FAASTeam) outreach.
➢ Seats and Seatbelts - how to fasten, unfasten, and adjust seatbelts and shoulder harnesses
➢ Air Vents - location of air vents and heating controls; show where air sickness bags are located
➢ Fire Extinguisher - location and explain how to use
➢ Exits/Emergencies - discuss exits, emergencies, and passenger actions taken in the event of an emergency
➢ Traffic and Talking - Discuss "Sterile Cockpit" and that passengers can aid in looking out for air traffic
➢ Your Questions

cards.question: What is the "5 Ps" check list and how would you apply it throughout a flight?
cards.answer:
A Single-Pilot Resource Management tool consisting of:
➢ The Plan - Contains the basic elements of cross-country planning, constantly reviewed and updated. Is the plan safe, smart, legal?
➢ The Plane - Is the aircraft suitable, airworthy, and appropriate for the flight?
➢ The Pilot - Use of the IMSAFE checklist continuously throughout the flight
➢ The Passengers - Are the passengers pilots? Rushed? Nervous? Excited? Drunk?
➢ The Programming - Do I know how to use the avionics in this aircraft? Have I programmed as much as I possibly can before departing? Do I know how to make adjustments in flight to the avionics if the plan changes?

Consistently evaluating each of these factors at key points, specifically during preflight planning, preflight inspection, prior to take off, midpoint of flight, prior to final descent, and prior to final allows for objective analysis of different safety factors.

cards.question: Explain the 3P model.
cards.answer:
The 3P model (Perceive, Process, Perform) is a simple, practical, and systematic ADM approach that can be used during all phases of flight.

➢ Perceive the given set of circumstance for a flight
➢ Process by evaluating circumstances impact on flight safety
➢ Perform by implementing the best course of action

cards.question: What are the hazardous attitudes identified in ADM training, and what's the antidote for each?
cards.answer:
Anti-authority: "Don't tell me."
Antidote: Follow the rules. They are usually right.

Impulsivity: "Do it quickly."
Antidote: Not so fast. Think first.

Invulnerability: "It won't happen to me."
Antidote: It could happen to me.

Macho: "I can do it."
Antidote: Taking chances is foolish.

Resignation: "What's the use?"
Antidote: I'm not helpless. I can make a difference.

cards.question: What is Single-Pilot Resource Management (SRM), and how does it differ from Crew Resource Management (CRM)?
cards.answer:
SRM is the art and science of managing all the resources, both on-board the aircraft and external sources, available to a single pilot. This includes:
➢ ADM, risk management
➢ Task management
➢ Automation control
➢ Situational awareness

In SRM, a single pilot is conducting all tasks and must be vigilant to avoid task saturation and overlooking items.

cards.question: Explain the DECIDE model.
cards.answer:
The DECIDE model is used as a continuous loop and provides the pilot with a logical way of making decisions:
➢ Detect (the Problem)
➢ Estimate (the Need to React)
➢ Choose (a Course of Action)
➢ Identify (Solutions)
➢ Do (the Necessary Actions)
➢ Evaluate (the Effect of the Action)

cards.question: What internal and external resources are available to you as a single pilot facing a difficult decision?
cards.answer:
Internal resources include:
➢ Person in the right seat - even a passenger can assist with certain tasks
➢ Verbal communication - look, touch, say. Talking out loud reinforces actions
➢ Checklists
➢ Supplements
➢ POH
➢ EFBs

External:
➢ ATC
➢ Flight services

cards.question: Describe a personal minimums checklist and how a pilot would utilize one.
cards.answer: A personal minimums checklist is an itemized checklist that includes both conditions of flight and recency experience a pilot fills out to help control and manage risk by identifying risk factors. The FAA recommends the checklist is carried in a pilot's flight bag and used during planning and immediately before initiating a flight. The below checklist can be downloaded for free from faasafety.gov.

cards.question: Explain how proficiency differs from currency.
cards.answer: Currency includes all legal requirements a pilot must meet in order to make a flight and all conditions associated with that flight including flying passengers, IFR, etc. Pilot proficiency on the other hand is a result of the recency of flying experience in similar conditions to the flight being made. A pilot may legally be able to fly passengers under IFR at night via regulations, but if that pilot only has the minimum legal requirements for the flight and has not conducted flights in similar conditions the pilot's proficiency is likely low. The Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge states "One of the most important concepts that safe pilots understand is the difference between what is “legal” in terms of the regulations, and what is “smart” or “safe” in terms of pilot experience and proficiency." Personal minimum checklists are a great way to objectively analyze proficiency.

cards.question: How can automation (autopilot, glass cockpit) both help and hurt situational awareness?
cards.answer:
Automation can help a pilot via:
➢ Consolidation of information into PFDs / MFDs, assistance in task management
➢ Greatly reduce workload

Automation can hurt a pilot via:
➢ Unfamiliarity increases workload
➢ Lack of flying ability
➢ Chance of creating large errors not caught by pilots
➢ Over reliance for safety of flight

The degree to which automation helps or hurts a pilot overwhelmingly depends on a pilot's familiarity with the technology in the aircraft.

cards.question: What are the 3 axis of an aircraft and what control surface controls movement around them?
cards.answer:
➢ Vertical Axis - Rudder
➢ Lateral Axis - Elevator
➢ Longitudinal Axis - Ailerons

cards.question: What happens to air pressure and density as altitude increases?
cards.answer: Air pressure and air density both decrease with increases in altitude.

cards.question: What is the Standard Datum Plane?
cards.answer: A theoretical plane where air pressure (corrected to 15 degrees C) equals 29.92 "Hg. The Standard Datum Plane provides pilot's a reference point when considering and calculating performance for an aircraft.

cards.question: What is Bernoulli's Principle?
cards.answer:
As the velocity of a moving fluid (liquid or gas) increases, the pressure decreases. As air flows over and under the wing, the air flowing over the wing must travel faster due to the airfoil shape, creating low pressure and ultimately lift.

Editor Note: This is the answer provided in the Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge as well as other well distributed sources. Although air above a wing does go faster than the air below the wing and there is low pressure above the wing and high pressure below the wing resulting in flight, the phenomenon of lift is incredibly complex. Recommend watching a video on YouTube titled "Doug McLean | Common Misconceptions in Aerodynamics".

cards.question: What is an airfoil?
cards.answer: A structure designed to obtain reaction upon its surface from the air through which it moves or that moves past such a structure.

cards.question: What are the four forces acting on an aircraft in flight, and how do they interact in straight-and-level, unaccelerated flight?
cards.answer:
➢ Thrust - the forward force produced by the power plant / propeller
➢ Lift - produced by the dynamic effect of air acting on the wing and perpendicular to the flight path through the wing's center of lift. Opposes the downward force of weight 
➢ Drag - a rearward, retarding force caused by disruption of airflow by the wing, fuselage, etc. and the creation of lift
➢ Weight - the combined load of the aircraft itself, the crew, fuel, cargo, baggage.

These forces are in equilibrium in straight and level unaccelerated flight.

cards.question: Explain the lift/drag ratio and why it matters for aircraft performance.
cards.answer:
The lift-to-drag ratio (L/D) is the amount of lift generated by a wing or airfoil compared to its drag. As the aircraft's Angle of Attack changes this ratio changes. The below photo shows this where:
➢ L/D - Lift to Drag Ratio
➢ CD - Coefficient of Drag
➢ CL - Coefficient of Lift

cards.question: What are the different types of drags? How does each change with airspeed?
cards.answer:
Induced Drag - Drag created as a result of producing lift which decreases as airspeed increases.

Parasitic Drag - all forces that slow an aircraft's movement. This drag is not associated with lift. Comprised of Form Drag, Interference Drag, and Skin Friction Drag and increases with airspeed.
➢ Form Drag - Parasitic drag generated by the aircraft due to its shape and airflow around it.
➢ Interference Drag - Comes from the intersection of airstreams that creates eddy currents, turbulence, or restricts smooth airflow
➢ Skin Friction Drag - The aerodynamic resistance due to the contact of moving air with the surface of an aircraft

cards.question: How are wingtip vortices formed?
cards.answer: High pressure air from under the wing flows to the low pressure air above the wing by spilling over the wingtip resulting in lateral flow.

cards.question: Describe wake turbulence avoidance procedures used behind a larger aircraft during takeoff and landing?
cards.answer:
During take off and departure rotate before the larger aircraft and stay above its flight path.

During approach and landing stay above the larger aircraft descent and land further down the runway.

cards.question: What is ground effect, and how does it affect an aircraft during takeoff and landing?
cards.answer:
Ground effect is the change in the 3 dimensional flow pattern around the aircraft as a result of the vertical component of airflow being restricted around the wing tip. This results in a reduction of Induced Drag and increased lift performance.

During take off, an aircraft may become airborne at a slower speed than what is required for lift and during landing an aircraft may remain airborne below normal stalling speeds as a result of this phenomenon.

cards.question: Explain the difference between static and dynamic stability.
cards.answer:
Static Stability - the initial tendency, or direction of movement, back to equilibrium. In aviation, it is the aircraft's initial response when disturbed from a given pitch, bank, or yaw.

Dynamic Stability - the initial tendency to return to equilibrium that the aircraft displays after being disturbed from its trimmed condition.

cards.question: What is a stall, aerodynamically speaking, and what factors affect the airspeed at which it occurs?
cards.answer: A rapid decrease in lift caused by the separation of airflow from the wing's surface brought on by exceeding the critical Angle of Attack. An aircraft's weight, aerodynamic configuration, load factor, air density, CG, and wing contamination can all effect stall speed.

cards.question: What is a secondary stall, and how does it differ from a accelerated stall?
cards.answer: A secondary stall occurs when a pilot recovers from an initial stall too abruptly (raising the nose too quickly) before regaining sufficient airspeed, causing the wing to exceed its critical angle of attack a second time. It differs from an accelerated stall, which occurs at a higher-than-normal stall speed due to increased load factor (e.g., in a steep turn or abrupt pull-up).

cards.question: What are the forces that contribute to left turning tendencies? Describe each of them.
cards.answer:
Torque - reaction to engine/propeller spinning clockwise (when viewed from pilots seat). An equal force attempts to rotate the aircraft in the opposite direction, counterclockwise

Corkscrew Effect (Spiraling Slipstrea) - Spiraling rotation of the slipstream exerts force on the left side of the aircrafts vertical tail surface, inducing a yaw to the right

Gyroscopic Effect - 90 degree offset force as a result of effective force applied by the propeller. 

Asymmetric Loading (P-Factor) - Downward moving blade produces greater lift moving the center of thrust to the right of the prop disc area, causing yawing moment toward the left around the vertical axis.

cards.question: What is load factor, and how does it change in a level turn at increasing bank angles?
cards.answer: Load factor is the ratio of the total aerodynamic lift produced by an aircraft's wings to its actual weight. As the wings accelerate the aircraft in a turn there is an increase in stress on the airframe as a result of increased horizontal lift. This can be seen in the below image.

cards.question: How do load factor and stalling speed relate to each other?
cards.answer: An aircraft's stalling speed increases in proportion to the square root of the load factor. Thus, an aircraft that normally stalls at 50 kts will stall at 100 kts with a load factor of 4.

cards.question: What does the Vg diagram show?
cards.answer: The Vg diagram  displays velocity versus G loads (load factors). It shows the Normal Operating Ranges, Caution Range, Structural Damage ranges, and structural failure.

cards.question:
What is the significance of VA (maneuvering speed)?

Is VA shown on altimeters?
cards.answer:
If flying slower than maneuvering speed under extreme conditions an aircraft will stall prior to any structural damage or failure occurs.

On traditional altimeters VA is often not displayed, however most modern PFDs will have it annotated on the Airspeed Tape.

cards.question: What is the relationship between airspeed and Rate of Turn? Airspeed and Radius of Turn?
cards.answer:
As airspeed increases, the rate of turn will decrease unless the angle of bank is increased. Because the aircraft is traveling faster, the circumference of the turn is larger and thus the aircraft required more time to complete the turn.

As airspeed increases, the radius of turn will increase unless the angle of bank is increased. This is an exponential relationship; if an aircrafts airspeed doubles the radius of turn will quadruple.

cards.question: What is a standard-rate turn, and how is it used in emergency instrument flying?
cards.answer: A standard-rate turn is a turn of 3 degrees per second, resulting in a 360-degree turn in 2 minutes. It provides a consistent, known turn rate a pilot can use with reference to the turn coordinator to safely reverse course. For example, a 180-degree turn out of inadvertent IMC can be accomplished without needing outside visual references.

cards.question: What are the different aircraft maximum safe load factor categories and associated Limit Load Factors??
cards.answer:
➢ Normal: +3.8 to -1.52
➢ Utility (mild acrobatics, spins): +4.4 to -1.76
➢ Acrobatic: +6.0 to -3.00

cards.question: What are the primary flight controls?
cards.answer:
Ailerons - controls movement about the longitudinal axis (bank)

Elevator - control movement about the lateral axis (pitch)

Rudder - controls movement about the vertical axis (yaw)

cards.question: What are the secondary flight controls, and what does each do?
cards.answer:
Flaps - common high-lift devices that change the camber of the wings

Leading Edge Devices - Direct airflow to the top of the wing to delay airflow separation at higher angles of attack

Spoilers - high drag devices to reduce lift and increase drag

Trim Systems - used to relieve pilot of the need to maintain constant flight control pressure

cards.question: Explain how a trim tab works and why it reduces control pressure rather than moving the control surface directly.
cards.answer: Trim tabs adjust the airflow around a control surface to increase or decrease lift created by an airfoil such as the horizontal stabilizer / elevator pair or the vertical stabilizer / rudder pair. These small changes in lift allow the pilot to relieve flight control pressure for pitch, yaw, and bank.

cards.question: What are the 4 strokes of a 4 stroke engine?
cards.answer:
Intake - Compression - Combustion - Exhaust

Intake - piston starts downward travel, intake valve opens and draws fuel-air mixture into cylinder

Compression - intake valve closes, piston moves to top of cylinder compressing the fuel-air mixture

Power - fuel-air mixture is ignited, forcing the piston downward creating power to turn the crankshaft

Exhaust - exhaust valve opens, piston moves to cylinder head to purge burned gasses

cards.question: How does engine cooling work on a typical air-cooled horizontally-opposed engine, and what happens if cooling airflow is restricted ?
cards.answer:
Air cooling is accomplished by air flowing into the engine compartment through openings in front of the engine cowling. Baffles route this air over fins attached to the engine cylinders, and other parts of the engine, where the air absorbs the engine heat. Expulsion of the hot air takes place through one or more openings in the lower, aft portion of the engine cowling. If cooling airflow is restricted, cylinder head temperatures can rise excessively, risking detonation and engine damage. In response to high EGT or rough operation of the engine, pilots should:
➢ Open cowl flaps (if equipped)
➢ Enrich mixture
➢ Reduce climb angle
➢ Increase airspeed

cards.question: What is detonation?
cards.answer:
An uncontrolled, explosive ignition of the fuel-air mixture within the cylinder's combustion chamber. This causes excessive temperatures and pressures which, if not corrected, can lead to failure of the piston, cylinder or valves. Common causes include:
➢ Lower grade fuel than specified
➢ Operating the engine with extremely high manifold pressure and low RPM (constant speed)
➢ High power settings with excessively lean mixture

cards.question: Describe the change in propeller blade angle from the hub to the tip?
cards.answer: The propeller angle of attack is greatest closest to the hub to account for a slower actual speed, decreasing in angle of attack towards the tip. This design allows for constant lift along the length of the propeller.

cards.question: What is the difference between a fixed pitch propeller and constant speed propeller?
cards.answer:
Fixed pitch propeller - cannot change the pitch of the blades; engine power is controlled by throttle and the tachometer is the indicator of engine power

Constant Speed Propeller - has 2 controls, throttle and propeller control. Once an rpm is selected by the propeller control, a governor adjusts the propeller blade angle as necessary to maintain selected rpm. Manifold pressure is controlled by the throttle and indicates engine power

cards.question: How do float type carburetors work?
cards.answer: Outside air flows through an air filter and then into the carburetor's Venturi, a narrow throat in the carburetor. This creates a low-pressure area that forces fuel to flow through a main fuel jet located at the throat. The fuel then mixes with the airstream and into the intake manifold and ultimately cylinders. The throttle controls the throttle valve that increases or decreases the amount of air-fuel mixture that flows into the intake manifold.

cards.question: What does mixture control do and why is it important?
cards.answer: Mixture control adjusts the amount of fuel that enters the fuel-air mixture, allowing a pilot to compensate for lower air density at higher altitudes and higher air density at lower altitudes. If the mixture is not leaned at lower air densities, the air-fuel mixture will be fuel rich and cause carbon build up in the cylinder and on the spark plugs. If the mixture is too lean at higher power settings, detonation may occur.

cards.question: What causes carburetor icing? When is it most likely to occur?
cards.answer:
➢ Carb icing occurs due to the effect of fuel vaporization and the decrease in air pressure in the venturi which causes a sharp temperature drop in the carburetor and ice to form on internal surfaces of the carburetor, limiting air-fuel mixture flow.
➢ Carb ice is most likely to occur when temperatures are below 70 degrees F and the relative humidity is above 80%.

cards.question: How does an aircraft's electrical system work, and what happens during an alternator/generator failure?
cards.answer:
➢ A battery is used to start the aircraft, at which point an alternator begins to provide electrical power to the aircraft and recharge the battery.
➢ If an aircraft alternator/generator dies, the aircraft's electrical components will continue to run until the battery dies. When the battery dies, the engine will continue to run due to the spark in the engine being provided by redundant magnetos (permanent magnet) but all other electrical components will fail. Most modern avionics contain backup batteries in the case of an alternator failure / dead battery scenario. The below photo displays a common magneto layout.

cards.question: What are the basic components of a light aircraft's electrical system?
cards.answer:
➢ Battery - provides power for starting and backup power
➢ Alternator/Generator - provides electrical power in flight and recharges the battery
➢ Bus Bar - distributes power to electrical components
➢ Circuit Breakers/Fuses - protect individual circuits from overload
➢ Master Switch - controls power from the battery/alternator to the electrical bus

cards.question: How does an Emergency Locator Transmitter (ELT) work, and how is it tested?
cards.answer: An ELT automatically or manually broadcasts a distress signal on 121.5/406 MHz following an impact (activated by a G-switch), aiding search and rescue in locating a downed aircraft. It may be tested during the first 5 minutes of any hour, limited to 3 audible sweeps, and must be inspected within 12 calendar months (or after 1 cumulative hour of use/50% of battery life).

cards.question: What colors are associated with each fuel type/grade?
cards.answer:
➢ Red - AVGAS 80
➢ Green - AVGAS 100
➢ Blue - AVGAS 100LL
➢ Colorless/Straw - JET A

cards.question: Why is sumping fuel during preflight important, and what is a pilot checking for?
cards.answer: Sumping fuel drains a small sample from the lowest points of the fuel system to check for water contamination (water sinks below fuel due to water having a lower density than AVGAS; water appears as a separate bead), sediment/debris, and to verify correct fuel color/grade.

cards.question: What type of brake system is typically found on light training aircraft, and how is it operated?
cards.answer: Most light aircraft use independently actuated hydraulic disc brakes on the main wheels operated by toe pressure on the top of the rudder pedals. As the pilot applies pressure, the caliper causes the brake pads to constrict around the brake rotor causing friction and slowing. This allows for differential braking to assist with ground steering.

cards.question: What must a pilot be cautious of when using an exhaust heating system?
cards.answer: Carbon monoxide poisoning. Many GA aircraft use exhaust shrouds as a mechanism to provide cabin heat; if holes are present in these shrouds CO from the exhaust manifold may be directly entering the cockpit

cards.question: Explain how the pitot-static system works and which instruments rely on it.
cards.answer: The pitot static system allows static air to be provided to the Airspeed Indicator, Vertical Speed Indicator, and Altimeter. The pitot-tube allows ram air to enter into the pitot-static system. The Airspeed Indicator, Vertical Speed Indicator, and Altimeter all use the static system; the Airspeed Indicator uese the Pitot Tube as well.

cards.question: List and describe the different types of altitude.
cards.answer:
Indicated Altitude - read directly from the altimeter when it is set to the current altimeter setting

True Altitude - vertical distance of the aircraft above sea level - the actual altitude. Expressed as feet above mean sea level (MSL)

Absolute Altitude - vertical distance of an aircraft above the terrain, or above ground level (AGL)

Pressure Altitude - altitude when altimeter setting window is adjust to 29.92 "Hg. Altitude above the standard datum plane. Used to compute density altitude, true altitude, true airspeed, other performance data

Density Altitude - pressure altitude corrected for non-standard temperature. Directly related to aircraft performance.

cards.question: How does the altimeter work?
cards.answer: The altimeter contains a series of sealed aneroid wafers evacuated to an internal pressure of 29.92" Hg. These wafers are free to expand and contract as the air pressure in the case changes with outside air pressure (provided by the static system). As the aircraft climbs, the pressure in the case decreases, allows the wafers to expand, and via a set of gears indicates an increase in altitude. As an aircraft descends and the static pressure increases, the wafers are compressed and a decrease in altitude is indicated.

cards.question: What is the Kollsman window?
cards.answer: A barometric pressure setting window that displays the altimeter setting adjusted via an adjustment knob for variations in atmospheric pressure. The altimeter is set to the local altimeter setting or field elevation (if local altimeter setting is not available) prior to flight.

cards.question: What happens during a flight from high to low pressure/temperature if the altimeter is not adjusted? Flight from low to high pressure/temperature?
cards.answer:
High to Low - Look out below. When flying from high pressure or temperature to low pressure or temperature the altimeter will indicate an altitude HIGHER than True Altitude (actual height over MSL)

Low to High - You're in the sky. When flying from low pressure or temperature to high pressure or temperature the altimeter will indicate an altitude LOWER than True Altitude

cards.question: How does the Vertical Airspeed Indicator work?
cards.answer: The Vertical Airspeed Indicator (VSI) case contains a diaphragm; both the case and diaphragm receive static pressure via the static port. The diaphragm receives unrestricted static air, while the case pressure changes via a calibrated leak. When the aircraft is at a constant altitude, the pressures inside the case and diaphragm are equal and the instrument indicates 0. When the aircraft climbs or descends, the pressure inside the diaphragm changes immediately, but due to the metering action of the calibrated leak the case pressure remains higher or lower for a short time, causing the diaphragm to contract or expand and the instrument to indicate a climb or descent.

cards.question: How does the Airspeed Indicator work?
cards.answer: The Airspeed Indicator (ASI) is a sensitive, differential pressure gauge that measures and promptly indicates the differences between pitot (impact/dynamic) pressure and static pressure. Static pressure enters into the case via the static port and static air lines, and within the instrument case a diaphragm is mounted and connected to the pitot tube. As the airspeed increases, dynamic pressure increases, causing the diaphragm to expand and the instrument to indicate a higher airspeed. As airspeed decreases, the difference in pressures becomes smaller, the diaphragm contracts, and a lower airspeed is indicated.

cards.question: What would you observe on the Airspeed Indicator, Altimeter, and VSI if the pitot tube became blocked but the static port remained clear?
cards.answer:
Blocked Pitot Tube, Open Drain Hole - Effects ASI only; ASI indicates 0 knots

Blocked Pitot Tube, Blocked Drain Hole - Effects ASI only; ASI behaves similar to altimeter, higher IAS at higher altitudes, lower IAS at lower altitudes

cards.question: What would happen to the Airspeed Indicator, Altimeter, and Vertical Speed Indicator if the static port became blocked?
cards.answer:
Vertical Speed Indicator - Constantly display +/- 0.

Altimeter - Constantly display the altitude at which the static port became blocked.

Airspeed Indicator, Blocked Pitot Tube and Static Port - ASI behaves similar to altimeter, higher IAS at higher altitudes, lower IAS at lower altitudes

Airspeed Indicator, Blocked Static Port only - ASI continues to operate but is inaccurate, indicating lower than the actual airspeed when the aircraft is operated above the altitude where the static port became blocked, indicating higher than the actual airspeed when the aircraft is operated below the altitude where the static port became blocked.

cards.question: What does each of the standard airspeed indicator color markings represent?
cards.answer:
➢ White Arc - flap operating range
➢ Green Arc - normal operating range
➢ Yellow Arc - caution range; fly in this range only with caution
➢ Red Line - Never exceed speed

cards.question: What are VS0, VFE, VS1, VNO, VNE and what are they indicated by on the ASI?
cards.answer:
➢ VS0 - Stalling speed in the landing configuration; Lower Limit of the White Arc
➢ VFE - Maximum speed with the flaps extended; Upper Limit of the White Arc
➢ VS1 - Stalling speed in a specific configuration, most often the power-off stall speed at maximum takeoff weight in the clean configuration; Lower Limit of Green Arc
➢ VNO - Maximum structural cruising speed; Top Limit of Green Arc
➢ VNE - Never Exceed Speed; Red Line

cards.question: What are VA, VLO, VLE, VX, VY?
cards.answer:
VA - Maneuvering speed, maximum speed at which the structural design's limit load can be imposed without causing structural damage (effected by weight)

VLO - Landing gear operating speed, Maximum speed for extending/retracting landing gear
