VLE - Landing gear extended speed, Maximum speed at which an aircraft can be safely flown with landing gear extended

VX - Best Angle of Climb, airspeed at which an aircraft gains greatest amount of altitude in a given distance

VY - Best Rate of Climb, airspeed that provides most altitude in a given period of time.

cards.question: What is best glide speed (Vg) and why is maintaining it important during an engine-out emergency?
cards.answer: Best glide speed is the airspeed at which the aircraft achieves the greatest forward distance for a given loss of altitude (maximum lift-to-drag ratio L/D Max). Maintaining it maximizes the distance an aircraft may fly to reach a suitable landing site.

cards.question: What phenomena occurs during an approach when airspeed decreases below Vg?
cards.answer: The aircraft enters the area of reverse command (pitch for airspeed, power for altitude), a flight regime in which flight at a higher airspeed requires a lower power setting and a lower airspeed requires a higher power setting in order to maintain altitude.

cards.question: Explain rigidity in space and precession — the two gyroscopic principles — and which instruments rely on gyroscopes.
cards.answer:
Rigidity in space refers to the principle that a gyroscope remains in a fixed position in the plane in which it is spinning.

Precession is the tilting or turning of a gyro in response to a deflective force.

The Attitude Indicator, Heading Indicator, and Turn Coordinator all rely on gyroscopes.

cards.question: What instruments rely on the vacuum system to power the gyroscope? What happens if the vacuum fails?
cards.answer:
The Attitude Indicator and Heading Indicator gyroscopes both rely on the vacuum system to function.

If the vacuum system fails, the instruments will become unstable, inaccurate, and possibly erratic. The below image displays a typical vacuum system that can be found on an aircraft.

cards.question: What instrument relies on an electrically powered gimbal?
cards.answer: The Turn Coordinator. This gimbal is canted to allow the gyro to sense both rate of roll and rate of turn.

cards.question: What are the common magnetic compass errors?
cards.answer:
Variation - The difference between true and magnetic North caused by variations in the Earth's magnetic field. Apply the true-to-magnetic conversion.

Deviation - Depends on the aircraft heading, caused by the aircrafts magnetic field (electrical currents, magnetized parts, and conflict with the Earth's magnetic field). Apply the deviation correction found on the compass card.

Dip Error - Caused by the downward pull of Earth's magnetic field. The compass is designed to only rotate in the horizontal plane. This error can lock the compass up at unusual attitudes.

Turning Errors - The compass will lead during a turn to the North, and lag during a turn to the South. Remember UNOS, Undershoot North, Overshoot South.

Acceleration Errors - The compass will indicate a false turn when on and East or West headings. Remember ANDS, Acceleration North Deceleration South. The compass will indicate a false turn to the North while accelerating on East - West headings, and will indicate a false turn to the South while decelerating on East or West headings.

cards.question: What are the main sections of a Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH)?
cards.answer:
Section 1 - General
Section 2 - Limitations
Section 3 - Emergency Procedures
Section 4 - Normal Procedures
Section 5 - Performance
Section 6 - Weight and Balance / Equipment List
Section 7 - Systems Description
Section 8 - Handling, Service, and Maintenance
Section 9 - Supplements (for optional equipment)
Section 10 - Safety Tips (optional)

cards.question: What is a Minimum Equipment List (MEL), and how does operating with inoperative equipment differ for an aircraft that has one versus one that doesn't?
cards.answer: An MEL allows aircraft to be operated with inoperative equipment determined to be nonessential for safe flight. MELs allow for the deferral of inoperative items/equipment and conduct of flight for specific N-numbered aircraft and operators. This is often more permissive than 91.205.

cards.question: What is a Kinds of Operations Equipment List (KOEL)?
cards.answer: A KOEL specifies the kinds of operations (such as VFR, IFR, day, night) in which the aircraft can be operated and installed equipment necessary for each flight. Inoperative equipment, when required by the KOEL for a particular type of operation, may not be deferred for that operation under 91.213.

cards.question: What is an Airworthiness Directive (AD)?
cards.answer: An Airworthiness Directive (AD) defines the authority and responsibility of the FAA for requiring necessary corrective action when unsafe conditions exists as a result of design defect, maintenance, or other causes. One very common AD is AD 2011-10-09, applying to almost all Cessna 150, 152, 172, 182, and 210. This AD requires seat track wear checks, locking pin engagement checks, seat rollers and axles checks every 100 hours or 12 calendar months. A common field solution is the inclusion of a secondary seat stop.

cards.question: What are the different types of Airworthiness Directives?
cards.answer:
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) - Allows the aviation public to comment on the AD (normally 30 to 60 days) prior to publishing the final rule

Final Rule - Mandatory actions pertaining to aircraft specified in the AD with specific effective dates and compliance timelines

Emergency ADs - Issued when unsafe conditions exists that requires immediate, urgent corrective action before further flight; takes effect immediately upon receipt and grounds effected aircraft immediately.

cards.question: Who is responsible for Airworthiness Directive compliance?
cards.answer:
The owner or operator of an aircraft is primarily responsible for maintaining that aircraft in an airworthy condition, including compliance with Part 39 Airworthiness Directives.

The Pilot in Command of the flight has the final responsibility to ensure the aircraft is in an airworthy condition prior to conduct of a flight.

cards.question: What is a Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin (SAIB)?
cards.answer: An information tool issued by the FAA to alert, educate, and make non-mandatory recommendations to the aviation community. SAIBs are commonly used as Pre-AD warnings, to announce approved Alternate Methods of Compliance for ADs, general education, and industry alerts. One example is SAIB CE-18-24, a companion to AD 2011-10-09 with FAA recommendations on solutions to the problem identified in the AD.

cards.question: How does excess weight affect an aircraft's performance, structure, and stability?
cards.answer:
Excess weight reduces flight performance in almost every respect, including the following:
➢ Higher takeoff speed
➢ Longer takeoff run
➢ Reduced rate and angle of climb
➢ Lower maximum altitude
➢ Shorter range
➢ Reduced cruising speed
➢ Reduced maneuverability
➢ Higher stalling speed
➢ Higher approach and landing speed
➢ Longer landing roll
➢ Excessive weight on nose or tail wheel

cards.question: Describe the general process for computing an aircraft's weight and balance.
cards.answer:
➢ Determine the weight of each item (empty weight, pilot/passengers, fuel, baggage) and its arm
➢ Multiply each weight by its arm to calculate its moment
➢ Sum all weights to get total weight, and sum all moments to get total moment
➢ Divide total moment by total weight to find the CG location
➢ Verify the resulting weight and CG fall within the aircraft's approved envelope/limits.

The below image is an example of W&B calculations.

cards.question: What happens to an aircraft's controllability if the center of gravity is too far aft? Too far forward?
cards.answer:
The CG being too Far Aft results in:
➢ A tail heavy condition
➢ Decreased longitudinal stability
➢ Reduced capability to recover from stalls and spins

The CG being too Far Forward :
➢ Nose heaviness, making it difficult or impossible to flare for landings
➢ Decreased longitudinal stability

cards.question: Define Arm.
cards.answer: The horizontal distance in inches from the reference datum line to the CG of an item. (+) if measured aft of the datum, (-) if measured forward of datum.

cards.question: Define Basic Empty Weight.
cards.answer: The standard empty weight plus the weight of optional and special equipment that have been installed.

cards.question: Define Center of Gravity.
cards.answer: The point about which an aircraft would balance if it were possible to suspend it at that point.

cards.question: What are CG limits?
cards.answer: The specified forward and aft points within which the CG must be located during flight. These are measured in inches from the aircrafts datum.

cards.question: What is the CG range?
cards.answer: The distance between the forward and aft CG limits indicated on the aircraft's specifications.

cards.question: What is the Datum (reference datum)?
cards.answer: The imaginary vertical plane or line from which all measurements of arm are taken.

cards.question: What is Licensed Empty Weight?
cards.answer: The empty weight that consists of the airframe, engine, unusable fuel, and un-drainable oil plus standard and optional equipment as specified in the equipment list.

cards.question: What is Maximum Ramp Weight?
cards.answer: The total weight of a loaded aircraft including all fuel.

cards.question: What is Maximum Landing Weight?
cards.answer: The greatest weight that an aircraft is normally allowed to have at landing.

cards.question: What is Maximum Takeoff Weight?
cards.answer: The maximum allowable weight for takeoff.

cards.question: What is maximum weight?
cards.answer: The maximum authorized weight of the aircraft and all of its equipment as specified in the TCDS for the aircraft.

cards.question: What is Maximum Zero Fuel Weight?
cards.answer: The maximum weight exclusive of usable fuel.

cards.question: What is moment?
cards.answer: The product of the weight of an item multiplied by its arm measured in pound-inches (in-lb)

cards.question: What is useful load?
cards.answer: The weight of the pilot, copilot, passengers, baggage, usable fuel, and drainable oil.

cards.question: What is the standard weight for a gallon of 100LL?
cards.answer: The standard weight of 100LL is 6.0 lb/US gal. Other AVGAS types also hover around the 6.0 lb/US gal. mark, however there are some small variations in other types of fuel that, if applied to a significant amount of fuel, can create a errors in weight and balance calculations.

cards.question: How does density altitude affect aircraft performance?
cards.answer:
As air becomes less dense (higher density altitude):
➢ Reduced power, the engine takes in less air resulting in a lower fuel-air mass used and a weaker combustion stroke (Note: even when mixture is adjusted for the correct ration there is still less mass)
➢ Reduced thrust, the propeller is less efficient in thin air as a result or less air molecules for the airfoil to interact with
➢ Reduced lift, the thin air exerts less force on the airfoils

cards.question: What is density altitude?
cards.answer: Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature. This value correlates aerodynamic performance in the nonstandard atmosphere to an altitude in the standard atmosphere and allows performance calculations to be conducted in different pressures and temperatures.

cards.question: What is the effect of temperature on density?
cards.answer: As temperature increases, density decreases. This results in a higher density altitude.

cards.question: What is the effect of humidity (moisture) on density?
cards.answer: As the water content of air increases (increased relative humidity), density decreases. This results in a higher density altitude.

cards.question: What is the region of reversed command, and why is flying in it during approach considered higher risk?
cards.answer: A region of flight in which a higher airspeed requires a lower power setting and a lower airspeed requires a higher power setting to hold altitude. This is where the phrase "pitch for airspeed, power for altitude" originates.

cards.question: How does runway surface, gradient, and standing water affect takeoff performance?
cards.answer:
➢ Runway Surface: Anything (grass, dirt, gravel, poorly maintained pavement) but a well paved runway surface will increase take off distance.

➢ Gradient: Positive gradient (upslope, uphill) will increase takeoff roll distance, while a negative gradient (downslope, downhill) will reduce time to accelerate and takeoff roll distance.

➢ Water: Reduces friction with the pavement but may cause hydroplaning (specific consideration for aborted takeoffs and landing)

cards.question: What elements comprise the atmosphere?
cards.answer:
Earth's atmosphere is composed of:➢ Nitrogen - 78%
➢ Oxygen - 21%
➢ Trace Gasses - 1%

cards.question: What are the different levels of the atmosphere and what altitudes are associated with each?
cards.answer:
➢ Troposphere - 0 ft - 40,000 ft
➢ Tropopause - Boundary layer between the troposphere and the stratosphere. Commonly associated with the jet stream and possible clear air turbulence
➢ Stratosphere - 40,000 ft - 160,000 ft
➢ Mesosphere - 160,000 ft - 280,000 ft
➢ Thermosphere - 280,000 ft to 350 miles.

These are approximate figures as the height of each layer changes depending on location, with the atmosphere being thinner over the poles

cards.question: In what atmospheric layer do most weather, clouds, storms, and temperature variances occur?
cards.answer: Most weather occurs in the troposphere.

cards.question: What causes most weather via creating atmospheric circulation?
cards.answer: Uneven heating of the Earth's surface. The sun warms the earth, and warm air rises and subsequently becomes less dense. As this warm air increases in altitude, it eventually begins to cool, causing the molecules to pack together more closely and becoming denser / heavier than warm air. This more dense cold air then sinks to replace the rising warm air.

cards.question: As altitude increases, what occurs to both air pressure and air density?
cards.answer: Air pressure and air density both decrease with increases in altitude.

cards.question: What is the Coriolis force, and how does it affect wind direction?
cards.answer: The Coriolis effect is the force created by the rotation of the Earth. This force deflects air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, causing it to follow a curved path. This standard and consistent deflection creates northeasterly trade winds in the north (predominantly between the equator and 30 degrees latitude).

cards.question: What defines standard sea level pressure and temperature?
cards.answer: Standard Pressure is defined as 29.92" Hg (1013 mb), and standard temperature is defined as 59 degrees F (15 degrees C).

cards.question: What is the standard pressure and temperature change per 1,000 ft increase in altitude?
cards.answer:
The average change in atmospheric pressure is a decrease of 1" Hg per 1,000 ft increase in altitude

The standard temperature change in temperature is a decrease of 2 degrees C per 1,000 ft increase in altitude

cards.question: In the Northern Hemisphere, describe the relationship between wind patterns and pressure systems.
cards.answer:
➢ High Pressure systems are characterized by clockwise rotation and an outward and descending flow of air from the area of high pressure

➢ Low Pressure systems are characterized by counterclockwise rotation and an inward and rising flow of air towards the area of low pressure

cards.question: What is a trough and how is one depicted on weather products?
cards.answer: A trough is an elongated area of relatively low atmospheric pressure or height. Troughs are most commonly depicted by a dashed brown line similar to the photo below.

cards.question: What is a ridge and how is one depicted on weather products?
cards.answer: A ridge is an elongated area of relatively high atmospheric pressure or height. Ridges are most commonly displayed as a zig-zag styled line similar to the photo below.

cards.question: What is an isobar and what does the gradient between isobars tell us about local weather?
cards.answer:
Isobars are drawn on a weather chart to depict lines of equal pressure, resulting in a pattern that reveals the pressure gradientor change in pressure over distance. Isobars that are closely spaced indicate a steep pressure gradient and strong corresponding winds. Isobars that are spaced further apart indicate a shallow gradient and light winds.

Isobars in the surface analysis chart depicted below are the light grey lines with corresponding pressures in millibars.

cards.question: What is wind shear?
cards.answer: Wind shear is defined as a drastic change in wind speed and/or direction. Although this can happen at any altitude, low level wind shear is exceptionally dangerous due to proximity of the aircraft to the ground and possible sudden changes in lift.

cards.question: What is a microburst?
cards.answer: The most severe type of low-level wind shear, a microburst is associated with convective precipitation into dry air at a cloud base. A microburst can be indicated by an intense rain shaft at the surface but virga at cloud base.

cards.question: Explain atmospheric stability.
cards.answer:
➢Atmospheric stability is the atmosphere's ability to resist vertical motion. In an unstable atmosphere, small vertical air movements tend to become larger that results in turbulent airflow and convective activity. Moist air is generally less stable than dry air due to water vapor leading to decreased air density. The combination of moisture and temperature determine the stability of an air mass and resulting weather.
➢Atmospheric stability is the primary factor influencing cloud type and vertical development.

cards.question: What is a temperature inversion?
cards.answer: A temperature inversion occurs when air temperature increases with altitude. Inversion layers are commonly shallow layers of smooth, stable air close to the ground. The temperature of air increases to an altitude that acts as a lid, keeping weather and pollutants trapped below.

cards.question: When are surface-based inversion layers most common?
cards.answer: Surface-based inversion layers most commonly occur on clear, cool nights. The surface of the Earth cools as a result of radiative cooling, and this cooler ground subsequently cools the adjacent air.

cards.question: What is the relationship between temperature and the amount of moisture the air can hold?
cards.answer: For every 20 degree F increase in temperature the amount of moisture the air can hold roughly doubles. Thus, a 20 degree F decrease in temperature roughly halves the amount of moisture the air can hold.

cards.question: What are the three states water can be found in the atmosphere? What are the phase changes called between each state?
cards.answer:
Solid, liquid, gas

➢ Solid to liquid - melting
➢ Solid to gas - sublimation

➢ Liquid to solid - freezing
➢ Liquid to gas - vaporization (evaporation)

➢ Gas to liquid - condensation
➢ Gas to solid - deposition

NOTE: melting, vaporization and sublimation ABSORB heat. Freezing, condensation, and deposition RELEASE heat

cards.question: Describe relative humidity.
cards.answer: Relative humidity (expressed as a percent) is the amount of moisture in the air compared to the total amount of moisture the air could hold at a specific temperature.

cards.question: What is dew point? What occurs when temperature drops to dew point?
cards.answer: Dew point is the temperature at which the air can hold no more moisture and thus is fully saturated. When this occurs, moisture begins to condense out of the air in the form of fog, dew, frost, clouds, rain, or snow.

cards.question: Describe the different ways air can reach its saturation point.
cards.answer:
➢ Warm air moves over a cold surface
➢ Warm air and cold air mix
➢ Air cools at night through contact with the cooler ground
➢ Air is lifted or is forced upward in the atmosphere

cards.question: What are the different types of fog and how do they form?
cards.answer:
Radiation Fog - typically found on clear nights with relatively low wind. The ground cools rapidly due to terrestrial radiation which in turn cools the air to its dew point.

Advection Fog - occurs when a layer of warm, moist air moves over a cold surface (common in coastal areas).

Upslope Fog - occurs when moist, stable air is forced up sloping land features and the air cools to its dew point.

Steam Fog (sea smoke) - forms when cold, dry air moves over warm water.

Ice Fog - occurs when temperature is significantly below freezing and water vapor forms directly into ice crystals (sublimates).

Precipitation Fog - warmer rain falls through a layer of cooler, drier air near the ground evaporating to increase the air's moisture level until it reaches 100% saturation.

cards.question: What are the classifications of cloud based on bases and what are the associated altitudes for each classification?
cards.answer:
➢ Low Clouds: Form near the Earth's surface and extend up to about 6,500 ft AGL
➢ Middle Clouds: Form around 6,500 ft AGL and extend up to 20,000 ft AGL
➢ High Clouds: Form above 20,000 ft AGL

cards.question: What are the different types of clouds?
cards.answer:
➢ Cumulus - heaped or piled clouds
➢ Stratus - formed in layers
➢ Cirrus - ringlets, fibrous clouds, also high level clouds above 20,000 ft
➢ Castellanus - common base with separate vertical development, castle-like
➢ Lenticularus - lens shaped, formed over mountains in strong winds
➢ Nimbus - rain-bearing clouds
➢ Fracto - ragged or broken
➢ Alto - middle level clouds existing at 6,000 ft to 20,000 ft

cards.question: What is an air mass?
cards.answer: Large bodies of air with generally uniform temperature and humidity that take on the characteristics of the surrounding area or source region. This occurs when the body of air remains relatively stagnant for a period of days or longer.

cards.question: Describe a warm front, as well as weather prior to passing and during passage.
cards.answer:
A warm front occurs when a warm air mass advances and replaces a body of colder air. Slower moving, typically 10 to 25 miles per hour. Slope of advancing front slides over the top of the cooler air and gradually pushes it out of the area. As the warm air rises cooling and condensation occurs.

Wx prior to passage:
➢ Cirriform or stratiform clouds
➢ Fog
➢ Thunderstorms likely to develop in summer
➢ Light to moderate precipitation is probable, usually in the form of rain, sleet, snow, drizzle
➢ Low ceilings
➢ Wind from south-southeast
➢ Cool

Wx with the passage of a warm front:
➢ Stratiform clouds are visible and drizzle may fall
➢ Poor visibility, improves with winds
➢ Temperature rises from the inflow of relatively warmer air

cards.question: Describe a cold front, as well as weather prior to passing and during passing.
cards.answer:
A cold front occurs when a mass of cold, dense, and stable air advances and replaces a body of warmer air. Cold fronts move more rapidly than warm fronts, progressing at a rate of 25 to 30 mph. The cold front stays close to the ground and slides under warmer air, forcing the less dense warm air over the cold air mass.

Wx prior to passage:
➢ Cirriform or towering cumulus clouds; cumulonimbus clouds may develop
➢ Rain showers may develop due rapid development of clouds
➢ High dew point
➢ Falling barometric pressure

Wx with the passage of a cold front:
➢ Towering cumulus/cumulonimbus
➢ Heavy rain showers with possible lightning, thunder, hail
➢ More severe cold fronts include tornados
➢ Poor visibility
➢ Gusty and variable winds

cards.question: Describe a stationary front.
cards.answer:
A stationary front occurs when the force of two air masses are relatively equal, resulting in the the boundary/front remaining stationary
➢ Stationary fronts effect local weather for multiple days as a result little to no movement
➢ Stationary fronts can result in a mixture of cold and warm front weather patterns

cards.question: Describe an occluded front.
cards.answer:
An occluded front occurs when a fast moving cold front catches up with slower moving front
➢ Occluded fronts are characterized by warm front weather immediately followed by cold front weather
➢ Cold front occlusion: fast moving cold front colder than front it catches
➢ Warm front occlusion: fast moving cold front warmer than front it catches

cards.question: What are the stages of a thunderstorm's life cycle?
cards.answer:
➢ Cumulus Stage: Lifting action of air begins, raising moisture and warm air as the cloud increases in vertical development. Continuous, strong updrafts prohibit moisture from falling.
➢ Mature Stage: This is the most violent stage, moisture begins to fall in form of rain or hail. Heavy downward motion of air begins. Updrafts continue with warm rising air, while downdrafts begin with cool descending air. These updrafts, downdraft, and severe turbulence all exist within and near the cloud. Lightning is most intense during the mature phase.
➢ Dissipating Stage: Vertical motion near the top of the cloud slows down and begins to spread, causing an anvil shape. The downdrafts spread out to replace updrafts needed to sustain the storm.

cards.question: What distance is recommended for aircraft to remain from a thunderstorm?
cards.answer: The FAA recommends pilots stay at least 20 nm from thunderstorms.

cards.question: What conditions lead to structural icing, and what are the different types?
cards.answer:
Supercooled water droplets freeze on impact with an aircraft.

➢ Clear Ice: Heavy, hard, gloss. Formed by large water droplets that impact the airframe and freeze slowly. Most dangerous type due to difficult to see and rapid change to airfoil it causes.

➢ Rime Ice: Milky white, rough, granular. Formed by small water droplets that impact the airframe and freeze instantly. Light weight but forms quickly, rough texture disrupts airflow increasing drag and decreasing lift

➢ Mixed Ice: A combination of clear and rime ice

cards.question: What is a METAR, how often are they issued, and how long are they valid for?
cards.answer:
➢ A METAR is an observation of current surface weather reported in a standard international format.
➢ METARs are typically issued hourly (near the top of the hour)
➢ Valid until the next report is issued.

cards.question: What is a SPECI METAR?
cards.answer: A SPECI METAR is issued between hourly reports whenever weather conditions change significantly (sudden shifts in wind, visibility, storms)

cards.question: What are the typical pieces of information in the METAR?
cards.answer:
➢ Type of report: METAR, SPECI
➢ Station ID (KILM)
➢ Date/Time in 6 digit group (DDTTTTZ)
➢ Modifier: AUTO for automated sources, COR used to indicate correction
➢ Wind: Direction wind from, velocity (09012G18, from 090, Velocity: 12 Gusting 18 knots)
➢ Visibility: in SM or RVR (3 SM)
➢ Weather: qualifiers and phenomenon (+TSRA BR is thunderstorms, mist)
➢ Sky Condition: sequence always AMOUNT HEIGHT (BKN 0008)
➢ Temperature Dew Point: Temp / Dew Point (18/12)
➢ Altimeter Setting: " Hg in 4 digit group (A3010)
➢ Remarks: Remarks section always begins with "RMK"

cards.question: What is a PIREP? Why are PIREPs valuable although not mandatory?
cards.answer: PIREPs, or Pilot Weather Reports, provide valuable information regarding conditions as they actually exist in the air which cannot be gathered from other sources. Pilots can confirm the heights and bases of clouds, wind shear, wind speed and direction, visibility, sky cover, turbulence, and any other weather condition.

cards.question: What do the following signify in a PIREP: UA, UUA, OV, TM, FL, TP, SK, WX, TA, WV, TB, IC, RM?
cards.answer:
➢ UA - Routine PIREP
➢ UUA - Urgent PIREP
➢ /OV - Location, often distance direction from NAVAID
➢ /TM - Time
➢ /FL - Altitude / Flight Level
➢ /TP - Type Aircraft
➢ /SK - Sky cover/cloud layers
➢ /WX - Flight visibility first, then conditions (RA, HZ, TSRA, etc.)
➢ /TA - Air temperature in C
➢ /WV - Wind direction and speed in knots
➢ /TB - Turbulence
➢ /IC - Icing
➢ /RM - Remarks

cards.question: What is a TAF? How often is a TAF valid for? How many times and at what times are TAFs updated?
cards.answer:
➢ TAF stands for Terminal Aerodrome Forecast, a weather forecast issued for a 5 SM radius around an airport.
➢ TAFs are typically valid for 24 hours, with some larger airports having a valid period of 30 hours
➢ TAFs are updated 4 times daily at 0000Z, 0600Z, 1200Z, 1800Z

cards.question: What are the typical pieces of information in a TAF?
cards.answer:
➢ Type of report, TAF or TAF AMD (amended forecast)
➢ ICAO ID
➢ Date/Time of origin (DDTTTZ)
➢ Valid Period Dates (DDTT/DDTT)
➢ Forecast Wind
➢ Forecast Visibility
➢ Forecast Significant Weather
➢ Forecast Sky Condition
➢ Forecast Change Group (FM indicates from; TEMPO indicates temporary)
➢ PROB##: a given percentage that the weather listed will occur

Example:
TAF
KPIR 111130Z 1112/1212
TEMPO 1112/1114 5SM BR
FM1500 16015G25KT P6SM SCT040 BKN250
FM120000 14012KT P6SM BKN080 OVC150 PROB30
1200/1204 3SM TSRA BKN030CB
FM120400 1408KT P6SM SCT040 OVC080
TEMPO 1204/1208 3SM TSRA OVC030CB

cards.question: Describe how to read a winds and temperatures aloft forecast. How often are winds aloft forecasts published?
cards.answer:
Winds and Temperatures Aloft Forecasts (FB) provide data for varying altitudes starting at 3000 feet and increasing by 3000 feet until 12000, then increasing by 6000 feet. A six-digit group includes the wind direction with reference to true north, wind speed in knots, and temperature in degrees Celsius. The format is DDVV+TT where DD indicates wind direction (270 displayed as 27), VV is wind velocity, and +TT (or -TT) is temperature. Notes:
➢When the forecast wind speed is calm, or less than 5 knots, the data group is coded 9900
➢If the wind speed is forecast to be greater than 99 kts but less than 199 kts the computer adds 50 to the direction and subtracts 100 from speed. 731960 indicates winds 230 degrees at 119 knots and temperature of negative 60 degrees C.
➢If the wind speed is forecast to be 200 knots or greater, the wind group is coded as 99 knots. 7799 indicates wind 270 degrees at 199 kts or greater.

cards.question: What is an AIRMET? How often are AIRMETs issued? How long are AIRMETs valid?
cards.answer:
➢ AIRMETs are inflight weather advisories of operational interest to all aircraft, with weather section phenomena potentially hazardous to light aircraft
➢ AIRMETs are issued every 6 hours with intermediate updates as needed
➢ AIRMETs are valid until the next issued AIRMET and no longer than 6 hours

cards.question: Can AIRMETs be modified prior to the next issue time?
cards.answer: Yes, unscheduled updates, amendments, and corrections are issued as necessary.

cards.question: What weather phenomena are included in an AIRMET?
cards.answer:
Forecasts of:
➢ Moderate icing
➢ Moderate turbulence
➢ Sustained surface winds 30 kts or greater
➢ Widespread areas of ceilings less than 1,000 ft and/or visibilities less than 3 SM
➢ Extensive mountain obscuration

cards.question: What are the different types of AIRMETs?
cards.answer:
AIRMET SIERRA:
➢ IFR
➢ Mountain obscurations

AIRMET TANGO:
➢ Turbulence
➢ Sustained surface winds 30 kts or greater
➢ Non-convective low level wind shear

AIRMET ZULU:
➢ Icing
➢ Freezing levels

cards.question: What is a SIGMET?
cards.answer: ➢ A SIGMET is an inflight advisory concerning weather potentially hazardous to all aircraft.

cards.question: What are the different types of SIGMETs and for each describe the weather associated, issuance schedule and maximum validity in hours?
cards.answer:
SIGMET (WS):
➢ Severe icing
➢ Severe / extreme turbulence or clear air turbulence
➢ Dust storms and sandstorms that lower surface or inflight vis to below 3 SM
➢ Volcanic ash
➢ Unscheduled, issued as needed
➢ Valid for 4 hours (6 hours for volcanic ash and hurricanes)

Convective SIGMET:
➢ Surface winds greater than or equal to 50 kts
➢ Hail at the surface greater than or equal to 3/4 inch in diameters
➢ Tornados
➢ Embedded thunderstorms
➢ Squall line or line of storms at least 60 NM long where thunderstorms affect at least 40% of its length
➢ Thunderstorms producing heavy or greater precipitation affecting 40% or more of an area spanning at least 3,000 square miles
➢ Bulletin scheduled and issued hourly at H + 55
➢ Valid for 2 hours

cards.question: What are the different weather briefings and how do they vary?
cards.answer:
Standard Briefing, Abbreviated Briefing, Outlook Briefing.

Standard Briefing. Most complete information, should be obtained prior to departure of any flight. Contains:
➢ Adverse conditions along route
➢ Briefer "VFR flight not recommended" (if appropriate)
➢ Synopsis, overview of larger weather picture
➢ Current conditions (if ETD greater than 2 hours, current conditions not included)
➢ En route forecast
➢ Destination forecast
➢ Forecast winds and temperatures aloft
➢ NOTAMs
➢ ATC delays
➢ Other information

Abbreviated Briefing. Shortened version of standard briefing to obtain updated specific information.

Outlook Briefing. Requested when ETD 6 hours or more away. Provides initial forecast information.

cards.question: What does a Surface Analysis Chart display?
cards.answer:
A Surface Analysis Chart depicts an analysis of the current surface weather. Surface Analysis Charts are transmitted every 3 hours and cover lower 48 states and include:
➢ High/low pressure areas
➢ Fronts
➢ Temperatures and dew points
➢ Wind directions and speeds
➢ Local weather
➢ Visual obstructions

cards.question: What does a Weather Depiction Chart display?
cards.answer:
Weather Depiction Charts detail surface conditions as derived from METARs and other surface observations. Weather Depiction Charts are transmitted every 3 hours and include:
➢ IFR, VFR, MVFR weather
➢ Fronts
➢ Troughs
➢ Squall lines
➢ Sky conditions

cards.question: What does a Significant Weather Prognostic Chart display?
cards.answer:
Significant Weather Prognostic Charts are available as Low-Level Prog Charts (surface to FL240), Mid-Level Prog Charts (10,000 ft MSL to FL450), and High-Level Prog Charts (FL250 to FL630)
➢ A forecast of aviation weather hazards, primarily intended to be used as a guidance product for briefing the VFR pilot. Issued every 6 hours with TAFs.
➢ Broken into 12 / 24 hour panes

Includes:
➢ Freezing level
➢ Turbulence
➢ Cloud ceilings
➢ Restricted visibility

cards.question: What is Flight Information Service - Broadcast (FIS-B)?
cards.answer:
Ground broadcast service provided through the Automatic Dependent Surveillance - Broadcast (ADS - B) Services network and frequency. Provides pilots / aircrew of properly equipped aircraft with:
➢ METARs
➢ SPECIs
➢ TAFs and AMD
➢ NEXRAD
➢ NOTAM (D) and FDC NOTAM
➢ AIRMETs
➢ SIGMET (WS) / Convective SIGMET
➢ Status of Special Use Airspace
➢ TFRs
➢ Winds and Temperatures Aloft
➢ PIREPs

cards.question: What is the largest limitation that exists with NEXRAD radar data displayed in the cockpit?
cards.answer: Latency; the information displayed is often 15 to 20 minutes old. See NTSB Alert SA-017

cards.question: What are the different resources available to pilots for airport information?
cards.answer:
➢ Aeronautical charts
➢ Chart Supplement U.S. (formerly Airport/Facility Directory)
➢ NOTAMs
➢ EFBs
➢ Automatic Terminal Information Service (ATIS)

cards.question: What is the Automated Terminal Information Service (ATIS)?
cards.answer:
An ATIS is a recording of local weather conditions and other pertinent non-control information including:
➢ Runways in use
➢ Specific ATC procedures
➢ Airport construction activity
➢ Closed runways, taxiways, areas
➢ Obstacles near the airfield
➢ Give a new alphabetic code each hour (ALPHA, BRAVO, etc)

cards.question: What is a displaced threshold, and how does it affect landing versus takeoff distance available?
cards.answer:
A displaced threshold is a threshold located at a point on the runway other than the physical beginning of the runway
➢ A displaced threshold reduces length available for landings on the runway with the displaced threshold
➢ This part of the runway is available for takeoffs in either direction
➢ This part of the runway can be used for landing rollout from the opposite direction.

cards.question: What are the lost communication (lost comm) procedures at a towered airport if your radio fails?
cards.answer:
➢ Remain outside of airspace until direction and flow of traffic is determined
➢ Continue to communicate, you may still be transmitting
➢ Squawk 7600
➢ Look for light gun signals
➢ Land in accordance with traffic flow

Note: If flying with 2 pilots and Bluetooth capable headsets at low altitude, one pilot may attempt to call the appropriate approach / tower via cell phone.

cards.question: What is Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B), and how does it improve traffic awareness compared to a transponder alone?
cards.answer:
ADSB is a surveillance technology being deployed throughout the NAS to facilitate improvements needed to increase the capacity and efficiency of the NAS while maintaining safety.
➢ ADSB has a faster update rate than current radar systems
➢ Allows ATC surveillance services into new areas
➢ Provides Traffic Information Services - Broadcast (TIS-B)
➢ Provides Flight Information Services - Broadcast (FIS-B)

cards.question: What is a Terminal Radar Service Area (TRSA)?
cards.answer:
➢ TRSAs are areas where participating pilots can receive additional radar services from controlling agencies.
➢ Primary airports within TRSA are busier Class D airports
➢ Participation in TRSA services are voluntary but highly encouraged

cards.question: What is a VFR terminal area chart and when would it be used?
cards.answer: Charts with a scale of 1:250,000 that provide more detailed display of topographical information and airspace information found in / around Class B airspace. A zoomed in sectional.

cards.question: What's the difference between pilotage and dead reckoning as navigation methods?
cards.answer:
Pilotage is navigation by reference to landmarks or checkpoints

Dead Reckoning is navigation solely by means of computations based on time, airspeed, distance, and direction.

A combination of visual checkpoints and time / distance / airspeed calculations creates redundancy in a flight plan.

cards.question: What is the difference between true heading, magnetic heading, and compass heading?
cards.answer:
➢ True Heading - the direction in which the nose of the aircraft points during a flight measured in degrees clockwise from true north
➢ Magnetic Heading - the direction in which the nose of the aircraft points during a flight measured in degrees clockwise from magnetic north
➢ Compass Heading - magnetic heading corrected for compass deviation (errors caused by the aircraft's own magnetic influences)

cards.question: What is a VOR? DME? VORTAC?
cards.answer:
VOR (Very High Frequency Omnidirectional Range): Provides magnetic bearing information to and from the station for the pilot. Provides direction only

DME (Distance Measuring Equipment): Often integrated with VORs and found in VOR/DMEs and VORTACs, measures in NM the slant range distance of an aircraft from a VOR/DME or VORTAC

VORTAC: VOR with military tactical air navigation (TACAN) installed

cards.question: What methods can a pilot use to check the accuracy of a VOR receiver, and what are the allowable tolerances for each?
cards.answer:
➢ VOT (VOR Test Facility) - CDI must center within +/-4 degrees with a TO or FROM indication
➢ Certified ground checkpoint - CDI must center within +/-4 degrees
➢ Dual VOR check (using two receivers tuned to the same VOR) - the two must not differ from each other by more than 4 degrees
➢ Certified airborne checkpoint - CDI must center within +/-6 degrees

cards.question: How does a pilot positively identify a VOR station is operating and tuned correctly?
cards.answer: A pilot checks a VOR is tuned correctly by listening for the station's Morse code identifier. In the case of the below photo for the New Bern VOR-DME the pilot would listen for "DOT, DOT DASH DASH, DASH DOT" found to the right in the VOR-DME information box.

cards.question: How do you track VOR passage?
cards.answer:
➢ As an airplane approaches a VOR there is increased needle sensitivity
➢ Upon passage, the TO/FROM flag flips
➢ If equipped with DME, distance to station will change slower and read the aircraft's altitude above the station upon passage

cards.question: How should a pilot correct back on course when tracking a VOR radial and drifting off course?
cards.answer: To correct drifting of a VOR course, a pilot would turn toward the needle (CDI) to intercept the desired course using a wind-correction angle sufficient to compensate for the drift, then reduce the correction angle once established back on the radial to maintain the course.

cards.question: How does a GPS work; how many satellites are required?
cards.answer:
➢ GPS is a satellite-based navigation composed of a network of satellites in orbit. A GPS receiver 
➢ A minimum of 4 satellites for a three-dimensional position

cards.question: What is RAIM, what is its purpose, how many satellites are required?
cards.answer:
➢ Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring, GPS receivers use RAIM to verify the integrity of signals received from the satellite constellation
➢ RAIM allows the GPS to determine if a satellite is providing corrupted data
➢ At least one additional satellite in addition to those necessary for navigation is required, thus, for a 3 dimensional position a minimum of 5 satellites for a three-dimensional position

cards.question: What is the purpose of filing a VFR flight plan?
cards.answer: A VFR flight plan alerts search and rescue services if an aircraft becomes overdue. If not closed within 30 minutes of the estimated time of arrival, search and rescue procedures may be initiated by Flight Service/ATC.

cards.question: What is VFR flight following, and how does a pilot obtain it?
cards.answer: VFR flight following provides traffic advisory services to VFR aircraft on a workload-permitting basis from ATC. A pilot requests this service by contacting the appropriate ATC facility, providing aircraft type, position, altitude, destination, and stating "Request VFR flight following".

cards.question: Describe the "5 Cs" a pilot can use if lost during a cross-country flight.
cards.answer:
➢ Confess - admit to yourself that you are lost/unsure of position
➢ Climb - for better visibility, radio/GPS reception, and to see more land marks
➢ Conserve - fuel and any other essential resources
➢ Communicate - contact ATC or Flight Service for assistance
➢ Comply - follow all controller instructions and headings

cards.question: What are the different types of hypoxia and what causes each?
cards.answer:
Hypoxic Hypoxia: insufficient oxygen available to the body as a whole. Can result from a blocked airway, drowning, or lack of oxygen at high altitudes.

Hypemic Hypoxia: blood is unable to take up and transport a sufficient amount of oxygen to the cells in the body. Results from oxygen deficiency in blood, and can be caused by reduced blood volume from severe bleeding, medical condition, or CO poisoning.

Stagnant Hypoxia: Not flowing, oxygen-rich blood in the lungs is not moving. Can result from shock, heart failure, or a restricted artery.

Histotoxic Hypoxia: Inability of cells to effectively use oxygen. This results most commonly from alcohol, drugs, or other poisons.

cards.question: What are the symptoms of hypoxia?
cards.answer:
➢ Cyanosis (blue fingernails and lips)
➢ Headache
➢ Decreased response to stimuli, increased reaction time
➢ Impaired judgement
➢ Euphoria
➢ Visual impairment
➢ Drowsiness
➢ Lightheaded or dizzy sensation
➢ Tingling in fingers and toes
➢ Numbness

cards.question: What is hyperventilation, and how can it be distinguished from hypoxia in flight?
cards.answer:
The excessive rate and depth of respiration leading to abnormal loss of carbon dioxide from the blood. This can lead to unconsciousness due to the respiratory system's overriding mechanism to regain control of breathing. Common symptoms include:
➢ Visual impairment
➢ Unconsciousness
➢ Lightheaded or dizzy sensation
➢ Tingling sensations
➢ Hot and cold sensations
➢ Muscle spasms

cards.question: What is spatial disorientation?
cards.answer: Spatial disorientation is the lack of orientation with regard to position, attitude, or movement of the airplane in space. The body uses 3 systems, the vestibular system found in the inner ear, the somatosensory system including skin, joints, and muscle, and visual system to ascertain orientation and movement in space. When these systems supply conflicting information to the brain, spatial disorientation may occur.

cards.question: What are some of the vestibular illusions that can lead to spatial disorientation?
cards.answer:
➢ The Leans: An illusion that the aircraft is in a slight bank when the wings are level. This often results from a sudden return to level flight following a gradual and prolonged turn that went unnoticed by the pilot.
➢ Coriolis Illusion: Occurs when a pilot has been in a turn long enough for the fluid in the ear canal to move at the same speed as the canal; a sudden movement in a different plane may set the fluid moving creating the illusion of turning or accelerating in a completely different axis.
➢ Graveyard Spiral: Pilot in prolonged coordinated, constant-rate turn may experience the illusion of not turning. Upon return to level flight, the pilot will experience the sensation of turning in the opposite direction causing the disoriented pilot to return the aircraft to the original turn.
➢ Somatogravic Illusion: Rapid acceleration, such as during takeoff, stimulates the otolith organs in the same way as tilting the head backwards. Gives the illusion of being in a nose-up attitude, especially in conditions with poor visual reference. Disorientation may cause the pilot to push the aircraft into a nose-low or dive attitude
➢ Inversion Illusion: An abrupt change from climb to straight-and-level flight can stimulate the otolith organs enough to create the illusion of tumbling backwards
➢ Elevator Illusion: An abrupt upward vertical acceleration, as can occur in an updraft, can stimulate the otolith organs to create the illusion of being in a climb.

cards.question: What are some common optical illusions during approach and landing, and how can you prevent errors caused by them?
cards.answer:
➢ Runway Width Illusion: A narrower-than-usual runway can create an illusion the aircraft is at a higher altitude than it actually is (leading to a low approach). A wider-than-usual runway can create an illusion the aircraft is at a lower altitude than it actually is (leading to a high approach).
➢ Runway / Terrain Slope Illusion: An up-sloping runway can create an illusion the aircraft is higher than it actually is (low approach). Down-sloping runways create an illusion the aircraft is lower than it actually is (high approach).
➢ Featureless Terrain ("Black Hole") Illusion: Approaches over water, darkened areas, or snow make the aircraft seem higher than it is, so pilots tend to fly too low.
➢ Water Refraction: Rain on the windscreen makes the horizon appear lower, so the aircraft seems higher and pilots tend to fly low.
➢ Haze: Makes the runway seem farther away and the aircraft higher, so pilots tend to fly low.
➢ Ground Lighting: Roads or trains can be mistaken for runway/approach lights; bright runway lights with few surrounding lights make the runway seem closer, so pilots tend to fly high.

Prevention:
➢ Anticipate illusions at unfamiliar airports, especially at night or in poor weather; check airport diagrams and the Chart Supplement for slope, terrain, and lighting
➢ Make frequent reference to the altimeter on every approach
➢ Use VASI/PAPI or an electronic glideslope when available, and the VDP on nonprecision approaches
➢ If possible, fly over an unfamiliar airport to inspect it before landing
➢ Watch for distractions and emergencies, and stay proficient

cards.question: What cause carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning? What are the symptoms and treatment for carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning in flight? Why is CO poisoning particularly important to most GA pilots?
cards.answer:
➢ CO attaches itself to the hemoglobin in blood 200 times more easily than oxygen, preventing oxygen from getting around the body, to include the brain
➢ Symptoms: Headache, blurred vision, dizziness, drowsiness, and/or loss of muscle power. Treatment includes opening windows and providing supplemental oxygen
➢ Many GA aircraft use exhaust shrouds as a mechanism to provide cabin heat; if holes are present in these shrouds CO from the exhaust manifold may be directly entering the cockpit

cards.question: What is decompression sickness (DCS), and how long should you wait to fly after scuba diving?
cards.answer:
Decompression sickness is a condition characterized by a variety of symptoms resulting from exposure to low barometric pressures that causess inert gases (mainly nitrogen) that are dissolved in body fluids and tissues to form bubbles. After diving:
➢ Flight up to 8,000 ft MSL: wait at least 12 hours after diving if no decompression stops were required, 24 hours if decompression stops were required
➢ Flight to 8,000+ ft MSL: wait at least 24 hours regardless of dive type

cards.question: What is night blind spot, and what scanning technique helps compensate for it at night?
cards.answer: The night blind spot results from the rods being 10,000 times more sensitive to light than cones, and therefore resulting in a blind spot in the center of vision (Central Blind Spot).

cards.question: What is the difference between the movement area and non-movement area of an airport, and why does it matter for ground operations?
cards.answer: The movement area (runways and taxiways) requires ATC clearance to enter or operate on at a towered airport; the non-movement area (ramps, parking areas) generally does not require clearance. The boundary is marked with a movement area boundary marking.

cards.question: What is a stopway or blast pad, and how is it different from usable runway?
cards.answer: A blast pad/stopway is a paved area beyond the runway that is not intended for normal use during takeoff/landing roll but may support the weight of an aircraft in an aborted takeoff or overrun; it is marked with yellow chevrons and is not included in published landing/takeoff distance figures.

cards.question: What class airspace surrounds the Wilmington International Airport (KILM) and what is its ceiling?
cards.answer:
➢Class D
➢ 2,500 ft MSL

cards.question: What is indicated by the grey rings around the Wilmington International Airport (KILM)?

cards.question: What is the length of the longest runway at Wilmington International Airport (KILM)?

cards.question: What is annotated by the large blue numbers throughout the sectional? How are these calculated?
cards.answer:
Maximum Elevation Figures
➢If terrain is the Highest Obstacle: FAA determines the height of the obstacle, adds the possible vertical error (most commonly 100 feet), adds a 200' buffer for uncharted natural or manmade obstacles, then rounds the figure up to the next highest hundred foot level.
➢If man made obstacle is the highest obstacle: The FAA determines the height of the obstacle, adds the possible vertical error (most commonly 100 feet), then rounds up to the next higher hundred foot level.

cards.question: What is the proper technique for an emergency descent, and when would one be used?
cards.answer: An emergency descent is used to rapidly lose altitude, such as during an in-flight fire, depressurization, or need to escape icing. Technique typically involves reducing power to idle, extending the appropriate configuration (gear/flaps per POH), and using a bank/pitch attitude to maximize the rate of descent while remaining within airspeed limits.

cards.question: What is the difference between declaring "Mayday" and "Pan-Pan," and how should either be transmitted?
cards.answer:
➢ Mayday - Repeated three times, indicates a distress condition requiring immediate assistance (life-threatening emergency)
➢ Pan-Pan - Repeated three times, indicates an urgency condition that is not immediately life-threatening but requires attention
➢ Both should be followed by aircraft type and identification, weather, pilots intentions and requests, present position, present heading, altitude or flight level, fuel remaining in minutes, number of people on board, other pertinent information.

cards.question: What are the standard emergency transponder codes, and what does each indicate?
cards.answer:
➢ 7500 - Hijacking
➢ 7600 - Loss of two-way radio communications
➢ 7700 - General emergency

cards.question: What is the below sign and what does it indicate?
cards.answer: Taxiway Location Sign. The aircraft is currently located on taxiway TANGO. Location signs are black with bold yellow lettering.

cards.question: What is the below sign and what does it indicate?
cards.answer: Runway Location Sign. Informs the pilot the aircraft is currently located on RWY 15. Location signs are black with bold yellow lettering.

cards.question: What is the below sign and what does it indicate?
cards.answer: Taxiway Location Sign collocated with Runway Holding Position Sign. The aircraft is on taxiway TANGO and at the Holding Position for RWY 18 - 36.

cards.question: What is indicated by the below airport marking?
cards.answer: Taxiway Direction Sign pointing towards taxiway ALPHA. Yellow signs with bold, black lettering are directional signs.

cards.question: You are on a taxiway and see the below photo. Describe where you are and the different taxiways the pilot is approaching.
cards.answer: You are located on taxiway ALPHA. Taxiway Echo runs perpendicular to ALPHA. FOXTROT runs at a 45 degree angle to ALPHA ahead of and slightly to the left of the aircraft; TANGO runs at a 45 degree angle to ALPHA ahead of and slightly to the right of the aircraft.

cards.question: What is shown in the below photo?
cards.answer: Enhanced Taxiway Centerline intersection with a Runway Holding Position Marking. Most commonly seen at larger airports, Enhanced Taxiway Centerlines extend for a maximum of 150 prior to the Runway Holding Position Marking to warn the pilot the aircraft is approaching the runway and should be prepared to stop.

cards.question: What is shown by the photo below?
cards.answer: Holding Position Sign for ILS Critical Area. This sign, accompanied by the ILS Critical Area Holding Position Markings, indicates the holding position for an aircraft when an ILS is in use.

cards.question: What airport marking is shown below?
cards.answer: ILS Critical Area Boundary Sign. Located adjacent to the ILS Holding Position Markings on the pavement to indicate the ILS critical area.

cards.question: What sign is shown below?
cards.answer: No Entry Sign. Aircraft are prohibited from entering a certain area.

cards.question: What does the below represent, and what are its considerations?
cards.answer: Displaced Threshold Markings. The area before the threshold cannot be used for landings, but is available for take offs from both directions and landing from the opposite direction

cards.question: What does the below represent, and what are its considerations?
cards.answer: Relocation of a Threshold with Markings for Taxiway Aligned with Runway. The area before the threshold cannot be used for landings, but is available for take offs from both directions and landing from the opposite direction.

cards.question: What is the below sign and what does it indicate?
cards.answer: Runway Holding Position Sign. Located at the holding position on taxiways or runways that intersect a runway.

cards.question: What is the below sign and what does it indicate?
cards.answer: Holding Position Sign for a Runway Approach Area. At some airports, it is necessary to hold an aircraft on a taxiway located in the approach area for a runway so that the aircraft does not interfere with operations on that runway.

cards.question: What is the below sign and what does it indicate?
cards.answer: Runway Boundary Sign / Holding Position Sign. When oriented as such on the question side of the card, provides a reference to the pilot that the aircraft is clear of the runway. When the pilot is met with 2 solid lines then 2 dashed lines, the pilot must hold short until clearance is received to proceed onto the runway.

cards.question: What is the below sign and what does it indicate?
cards.answer: Runway Distance Remaining Sign. Seen along one or both sides of the runway, indicates the distance remaining in thousands of feet. In the case of this card, there are 3,000 ft remaining of runway. Note: the final sign, "1", will be located at least 950 ft from the runway end.

cards.question: What is the below sign and what does it indicate?
cards.answer: Holding Position Sign at Beginning of a Takeoff Runway. The pilot and aircraft are about to enter RWY 33 at the departure end.

cards.question: What is displayed in the below photo, and what does each different variation represent?
cards.answer:
2-Bar Visual Approach Slope Indicator (VASI) providing one visual glide path which is normally set to 3 degrees. These lights are visible out to 3-5 miles during day and up to 20+ miles at night. The visual glide path provides safe obstruction clearance within plus or minus 10 degrees of the extended runway centerline and up to 4NM from the runway threshold.
➢Top - RED, Bottom - RED: Below glide slope
➢Top - RED, Buttom - WHITE: On glidegslope
➢Top - WHITE, Bottom - WHITE: Above glide slope

cards.question: What is displayed in the below photo, and what does each different variation represent?
cards.answer:
Precision Approach Path Indicator (PAPI). Similar to VASI, lights installed in single row. Visible for 5 miles during day and up to 20 miles at night. PAPIs provide safe obstruction clearance within plus or minus 10 degrees of the extended runway centerline and up to 3.4 NM from the runway threshold.
➢WHITE - WHITE - WHITE - WHITE: High (more than 3.5 degrees)
➢WHITE - WHITE - WHITE - RED: Slightly High (3.2 degrees)
➢WHITE - WHITE - RED - RED: On Glide Path (3 degrees)
➢ WHITE - RED - RED - RED: Slightly Low (2.8 degrees)
➢RED - RED - RED - RED: Low (less than 2.5 degrees)

cards.question: What are the eligibility requirements to apply for a Commercial Pilot Certificate?
cards.answer:
To be eligible for a commercial pilot certificate, a person must:
(a) Be at least 18 years of age
(b) Be able to read, speak, write, and understand the English language.
(c) Receive a logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor who: (1) Conducted the required ground training or reviewed the person's home study and; (2) Certified that the person is prepared for the required knowledge test that applies to the aircraft category and class rating sought.
(d) Pass the required knowledge test
(e) Receive the required aeronautical training and a logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor who: (1) Conducted the training (2) Certified that the person is prepared for the required practical test. 
(f) Meet the aeronautical experience requirements of this subpart that apply to the aircraft category and class rating sought;
(g) Pass the required practical test
(h) Hold at least a private pilot certificate
(i) Comply with the sections of this part that apply to the aircraft category and class rating sought.

cards.question: What are the minimum aeronautical experience requirements for a Commercial Pilot certificate, airplane single-engine land?
cards.answer:
For a commercial pilot certificate with an airplane category and single-engine class rating must log at least 250 hours of flight time as a pilot that consists of at least:
(1) 100 hours in powered aircraft, of which 50 hours must be in airplanes.
(2) 100 hours of pilot-in-command flight time, which includes at least— (i) 50 hours in airplanes; and (ii) 50 hours in cross-country flight of which at least 10 hours must be in airplanes.
(3) 20 hours of training on the areas of operation listed in § 61.127(b)(1) of this part that includes at least—
  (i) Ten hours of instrument training using a view-limiting device including attitude instrument flying, partial panel skills, recovery from unusual flight attitudes, and intercepting and tracking navigational systems. Five hours of the 10 hours required on instrument training must be in a single engine airplane;
  (ii) 10 hours of training in a complex airplane, a turbine-powered airplane, or a technically advanced airplane (TAA) that meets the requirements of paragraph (j) of this section, or any combination thereof.
  (iii) One 2-hour cross country flight in a single engine airplane in daytime conditions that consists of a total straight-line distance of more than 100 nautical miles from the original point of departure;
 (iv) One 2-hour cross country flight in a single engine airplane in nighttime conditions that consists of a total straight-line distance of more than 100 nautical miles from the original point of departure; and
    (v) Three hours in a single-engine airplane with an authorized instructor in preparation for the practical test within the preceding 2 calendar months from the month of the test.
(4) Ten hours of solo flight time in a single engine airplane or 10 hours of flight time performing the duties of pilot in command in a single engine airplane with an authorized instructor on board (either of which may be credited towards the flight time requirement under paragraph (a)(2) of this section), on the areas of operation listed under § 61.127(b)(1) that include—
   (i) One cross-country flight of not less than 300 nautical miles total distance, with landings at a minimum of three points, one of which is a straight-line distance of at least 250 nautical miles from the original departure point. However, if this requirement is being met in Hawaii, the longest segment need only have a straight-line distance of at least 150 nautical miles; and
  (ii) 5 hours in night VFR conditions with 10 takeoffs and 10 landings (with each landing involving a flight in the traffic pattern) at an airport with an operating control tower.

cards.question: Does a commercial pilot certificate expire?
cards.answer: No, pilot certificates are issued without expiration dates.

cards.question: When may a pilot act as Second in Command (SIC)?
cards.answer:
A person may serve as second-in-command of an aircraft type certificated for more than one required pilot flight crewmember only if that person:
(1) Holds at least a private pilot certificate with the appropriate category and class rating;
(2) Holds an instrument rating or privilege that applies to the aircraft being flown if the flight is under IFR;
(3) Holds at least a pilot type rating for the aircraft being flown unless the flight will be conducted as domestic flight operations within the United States airspace

Additionally, within the preceding 12 months;
(1) Become familiar with the following information for the specific type aircraft for which second-in-command privileges are requested—
  (i) Operational procedures applicable to the powerplant, equipment, and systems.
  (ii) Performance specifications and limitations.
  (iii) Normal, abnormal, and emergency operating procedures.
   (iv) Flight manual.
    (v) Placards and markings.
(2) Except as provided in paragraph (g) of this section, performed and logged pilot time in the type of aircraft or in a flight simulator that represents the type of aircraft for which second-in-command privileges are requested, which includes—
  (i) Three takeoffs and three landings to a full stop as the sole manipulator of the flight controls;
  (ii) Engine-out procedures and maneuvering with an engine out while executing the duties of pilot in command; and
   (iii) Crew resource management training.

cards.question: What happens to a pilot's certificate if a alcohol test is refused?
cards.answer:
A refusal to submit to a test to indicate the percentage by weight of alcohol in the blood or a refusal to furnish or authorize the release of the test results requested by the FAA is grounds for:
(a) Denial of an application for any certificate, rating, or authorization issued under this part for a period of up to 1 year after the date of that refusal; or
(b) Suspension or revocation of any certificate, rating, or authorization issued under this part.

cards.question: What privileges may a pilot exercise when holding a Commercial Pilot Certificate?
What limitations are placed on a commercial pilot who does not hold an instrument rating?
cards.answer:
If the holder of a commercial pilot certificate does not hold an instrument rating in the same category and class the following are prohibited. The carriage of passengers for hire
➢on cross-country flights in excess of 50 NM
➢At night.

cards.question: Define "common carriage"; what four elements are associated with common carriage?
cards.answer:
In AC 120-12A, the FAA states that a carrier becomes a common carrier when it "holds itself out" to the public, or to a segment of the public, as willing to furnish transportation within the limits of its facilities to any person who wants it. There are 4 elements in defining a common carrier:
(1) the holding out of a willingness to
(2) transport persons or property
(3) from place to place
(4)for compensation.

cards.question: What constitutes "holding out", and what are some examples of holding out?
cards.answer:
"Holding out" is accomplished by any means that communicates to the public that a transportation service is indiscriminately available to the members of that segment of the public that it is designed to attract. There is no specific rule or criteria; instead, holding out is determined by assessing the available facts. Holding out can be done in many ways, including:
➢Signs and advertising
➢Use of agents, agencies, or salespeople
➢Print publications
➢Internet
➢Websites
➢Social Media
➢Mobile device applications
➢Emails
➢Personal solicitations and reputation
➢Course of conduct

cards.question: What is private carriage? How does it differ from common carriage?
cards.answer:
Private carriage is carriage for hire which does not involve "holding out". Private carriage for hire is carriage for one or several selected customers, generally on a long-term basis. The number of contracts must not be too great as to imply a willingness to contract with anybody.

Unlike in common carriage, operators conducting private carriage do not hold themselves out as willing to furnish transportation to anybody.

cards.question: What is noncommon carriage?
cards.answer:
14 CFR 110.2 defines noncommon carriage as "any aircraft operation for compensation or hire that does not involve a holding out to others." 

To distinguish, noncommon carriage is the 14 CFR 110.2 definition while private carriage is the common-law term and legal interpretation disseminated via AC 120-12A.

cards.question: What is the purpose of 14 CFR 119?
cards.answer:
Part 119 prescribes the operating certificates, certification requirements, and operating requirements for Part 121, Part 125, and Part 135. This includes:
(1) The types of operator certificates issued by the FAA, including air carrier and operation certificates,
(2) The certification requirements an operator must meet to operate under part 121, part 125, or part 135
(3) The requirements an operator must meet to conduct operations under part 121, 125, or 135
(4) Requirements affecting wet leasing
(5) Requirements for deviation authority under a military contract
(6) Management personnel requirements when operating under Part 121 or Part 135

cards.question: What is the difference between a wet lease and dry lease? Why is this important for a commercial pilot to understand?
cards.answer:
The FAA defines a wet lease in Part 110.2 as "any leasing arrangement whereby a person agrees to provide an entire aircraft and at least one crewmember." During a wet lease the lessor maintains operational control. Part 119.53 goes on to restrict the conduct of wet leasing aircraft to certificate holders authorized to conduct common carriage operations under Part 119.

A dry lease is the leasing of an aircraft without crewmembers. The lessee exercises operational control of the aircraft and no Part 119 operating certificate is required as long as the lessee does not carry persons or property for hire. Larger aircraft operating considerations can be found in Part 125.

cards.question: As a commercial pilot, may you provide both the airplane and services as a pilot to carry a passenger for hire?
cards.answer: No, this would constitute a wet lease and would require an operating certificate issued under Part 119.

cards.question: Are there operational exceptions to Part 119 certification requirements?
May a commercial pilot conduct sight seeing flights for compensation? Is additional preparatory action required by the pilot? Are any restrictions placed on site seeing flights?
cards.answer:
Yes, a pilot may conduct site seeing flight for compensation. The pilot must have obtained and conduct the flight in accordance with a Letter of Authorization issued under 91.147 and the following limitation apply:
(1) Must be nonstop
(2) The aircraft must have a passenger-seat configuration of 30 seats or less and a maximum capacity of 7,500 pounds
(3) The flight must begin and end at the same airport
(4) The full flight must be conducted within a 25 NM radius from that airport.

cards.question: What additional requirements exist for banner towing operations?
cards.answer: To conduct banner towing operations, a pilot must apply for and obtain a Certificate of Waiver (CoW) J5500, Banner Towing Operations (FAA Form 7711-2 is the Application for Certificate of Waiver or Authorization). The pilot must then demonstrate competency to an FAA Aviation Safety Inspector (as indicated in SAFO 15002) including at least one pickup and one drop off the largest banner the operator intends to fly. Upon completion the CoW is issued to the operator/entity.

cards.question: What is the FAA's definition of "compensation"?
cards.answer: The FAA construes "compensation or hire" very broadly. It does not require a profit, a profit motive, or the actual payment of funds. Instead, compensation under the FAA's view is the receipt of anything of value
cards.ref: FAA Legal Interpretation to Mr. Joseph Kirwan

cards.question: May a pilot carry passengers for hire in an airplane holding an experimental, restricted, or light-sport special airworthiness certificate?
cards.answer: Overwhelmingly no, although there are some specific instances for experimental, restricted, and light-sport aircraft the FAA has deemed that flights for compensation or hire in these aircraft cannot be conducted. For additional details, consult 91.313 (restricted), 91.319 (experimental), and 91.327 (light-sport)

cards.question: What are the Airframe and Powerplant certification requirements for annual and 100 hour inspections?
cards.answer: Any Airframe and Powerplant (A&P) mechanic is authorized to conduct and approve return to service after 100-hour inspections. Annual inspections must be conducted by an A&P with Inspection Authorization (often referred to as IA).

cards.question: What is a progressive inspection and when would an operator use one?
cards.answer:
Progressive inspections must be approved by the responsible Flight Standards Office and allows the operator of an aircraft to conduct continuous maintenance on an aircraft and powerplant in alignment with a submitted detailed inspection schedule. This allows for more consistent maintenance and repairs in lieu of larger more time consuming inspections. Should the progressive inspection schedule not be adhered to, the next annual will be due 12 months from the last complete inspection and next 100-hour inspection will be due 100 hours after the last complete inspection.

A complete inspection of the aircraft, for the purpose of determining when the annual and 100-hour inspections are due, requires a detailed inspection of the aircraft and all its components in accordance with the progressive inspection.

cards.question: What is a Service Bulletin? Is compliance to Service Bulletins mandatory?
cards.answer:
Manufacturers issue aircraft Service Bulletins (SB) to inform owners and operators about critical and useful information on aircraft safety, maintenance, or product improvement. Compliance with SBs may or may not be mandatory, but pilot's should never ignore them when it comes to safety.

If a pilot is operating under 14 CFR 91, a SB is advisory and compliance is not mandatory UNLESS it is included in an Airworthiness Directive.
cards.ref: Service Bulletins and the Aircraft Owner (FAASTeam Fact Sheet)

cards.question: Does an aircraft being operated for hire change a pilot's ability to perform preventative maintenance?
cards.answer:
Yes, depending on the type of operations the aircraft is being used for. Pilots flying aircraft via a Part 121, 129, or 135 operating certificate are not authorized to conduct preventative maintenance on that aircraft.

Exact 14 FAR 43.3(g) verbiage: Except for holders of a sport pilot certificate, the holder of a pilot certificate issued under part 61 may perform preventive maintenance on any aircraft owned or operated by that pilot which is not used under part 121, 129, or 135 of this chapter. The holder of a sport pilot certificate may perform preventive maintenance on an aircraft owned or operated by that pilot and issued a special airworthiness certificate in the light-sport category.

cards.question: Once an Minimum Equipment List is approved and issued does it become a required document aboard the aircraft?
cards.answer: Yes, the pilot must have onboard the aircraft both the letter of authorization issued by the responsible Flight Standards office authorizing  operation of the aircraft under the MEL. The MEL and letter of authorization constitute a supplemental type certificate for the aircraft.

cards.question: What is a commercial operator?
cards.answer:
Commercial operator means a person who, for compensation or hire, engages in the carriage by aircraft in air commerce of persons or property, other than as an air carrier or foreign air carrier or under the authority of Part 375. Where it is doubtful that an operation is for "compensation or hire", the test applied is whether the carriage by air is merely incidental to the person's other business or is, in itself, a major enterprise for profit.

Commercial operator is a broader, catch-all category distinct from "air carrier" for all other persons or businesses that are being compensate for carriage but might not necessarily be holding out. This is a regulatory means of pulling noncommon and private carriage to require Part 119 certification requirements.

cards.question: What is operational control of an aircraft?
cards.answer:
Operational control is the exercise of authority over initiating, conducting, or terminating a flight.

In Part 121/135 operations the certificate holder keeps operational control and must list in its manual each person authorized to exercise it (for example the director of operations, dispatcher/flight follower, and PIC). The PIC is still directly responsible for, and the final authority as to, the operation of the aircraft (91.3).

Who holds operational control is the key test for an illegal charter: if the person who provides the aircraft (and often the pilot) also controls the flight and is paid for the transportation, it is a commercial operation that requires a Part 119 certificate.

cards.question: What are the different types of operations that require a Part 119 certificate?
cards.answer:
There are five "kinds of operation" a Part 119 certificate holder can be authorized to conduct:

Conducted under Part 121:
➢ Domestic – scheduled operations in turbojets, or airplanes with more than 9 passenger seats or more than 7,500 lb payload, within the 48 contiguous states/D.C. (or within one state, territory, or possession)
➢ Flag – the same kind of scheduled operation, but between the U.S. and points outside the U.S. (or between two points outside the U.S.)
➢ Supplemental – common carriage in larger airplanes (more than 30 passenger seats or more than 7,500 lb payload) with negotiated departure times, all-cargo, or public charters

Conducted under Part 135:
➢ Commuter – scheduled operations (at least 5 round trips per week on at least one route) in rotorcraft or non-turbojet airplanes with 9 or fewer passenger seats and 7,500 lb or less payload
➢ On-demand – charter-type operations with negotiated departure times (and limited small scheduled or all-cargo operations) in smaller aircraft

cards.question: What commercial operations do not require a Part 119 certificate? (Note: not looking for the exempt operations list in 119.1(e).)
cards.answer:
Operations that are excluded from Part 119 because they are certificated or governed under other rules, or because they are not common carriage:

➢ Part 91 Subpart K fractional ownership operations (when common carriage is not involved)
➢ Part 133 rotorcraft external-load and Part 137 agricultural operations – these have their own operating certificates
➢ Part 129 operations by foreign air carriers
➢ Part 91 Subpart F operations of large and turbine-powered multiengine airplanes listed in 91.501(b) (e.g., time-sharing, interchange, and joint-ownership agreements, and carrying company officials/guests incidental to the company's business), when common carriage is not involved
➢ Corporate flight departments where the air transportation is merely incidental to the company's other business rather than a major enterprise for profit – the 14 CFR 1.1 test for whether someone is a "commercial operator"

Note: Noncommon or private carriage for compensation in an aircraft with fewer than 20 seats and less than 6,000 lb payload still requires a Part 119 certificate and Part 135 rules (119.23(b)), except for the 91.501(b) operations above.

cards.question: What are the 2 basic types of operating certificates that are issued under Part 119?
cards.answer:
1. Air Carrier Certificate – issued to a person authorized to conduct operations as a direct air carrier (common carriage).

2. Operating Certificate – issued to a person authorized to operate as a U.S. commercial operator but not as a direct air carrier, and to operators of airplanes with 20 or more passenger seats or 6,000 lb or more payload capacity when common carriage is not involved.

cards.question: How is local time converted to UTC?
cards.answer:
Add the time zone's offset to local time. FAA uses Coordinated Universal Time (UTC, also called "Zulu") on a 24-hour clock for all operations.

Standard time → UTC:
➢ Eastern: add 5 hours
➢ Central: add 6 hours
➢ Mountain: add 7 hours
➢ Pacific: add 8 hours
➢ Alaska: add 9 hours
➢ Hawaii: add 10 hours

During daylight saving time, subtract 1 hour from these values (e.g., EDT + 4 hours = UTC). Remember the date also changes when the conversion passes 2400Z.

Example: 1500 EDT + 4 = 1900Z.

cards.question: Explain what the following mean in a TAF: TEMPO, BECMG, FM, PROB30.
cards.answer:
➢ FM (From) – a rapid, significant change to a new set of conditions beginning at the stated time (FMDDHHMM). All conditions on that line replace the previous forecast.
