➢ TEMPO (Temporary) – temporary fluctuations expected to last less than 1 hour at a time and, in total, less than half of the stated period (DDHH/DDHH).
➢ BECMG (Becoming) – a gradual change to the new conditions expected sometime during the stated period; the new conditions then persist.
➢ PROB30 – a 30% probability of the stated conditions (usually thunderstorms or precipitation) occurring during the stated period. (PROB40 = 40%.)

cards.question: What is the Graphical Forecast for Aviation (GFA), how often is the GFA updated, and how long is the future window projected out?
cards.answer:
The GFA is a set of web-based displays from the NWS Aviation Weather Center (aviationweather.gov) that shows observations, forecasts, and warnings for the CONUS on one interactive map. In 2017 it replaced the textual Area Forecast (FA) for the CONUS.

➢ Forecast tabs: ceiling & visibility, clouds, precipitation, thunderstorms, temperature, winds, turbulence, and icing
➢ Observation/warning overlays: METARs, PIREPs, satellite, radar, lightning, SIGMETs, G-AIRMETs, CWAs, TAFs

Updates: the products update continuously – observations and ceiling/visibility analysis as often as every 15 minutes, model forecast fields each hour.

Time window: the GFA can be viewed from 18 hours in the past to 18 hours in the future (hourly forecast steps).
cards.ref: aviationweather.gov GFA Help; Aviation Weather Handbook (FAA-H-8083-28B) Chapter 28

cards.question: What is a Convective Outlook?
cards.answer:
A Convective Outlook (AC) is a national forecast from the NWS Storm Prediction Center (SPC) of the potential for severe thunderstorms (tornadoes, wind gusts of 50 knots or greater, large hail) and general (non-severe) thunderstorms across the CONUS. It is a flight-planning tool, not an in-flight advisory.

➢ Day 1 – issued 5 times daily (0600Z, 1300Z, 1630Z, 2000Z, 0100Z)
➢ Day 2 – issued twice daily; Day 3 – issued twice daily
➢ Days 4–8 – issued once daily

Risk categories: TSTM (general thunderstorms), 1-MRGL (marginal), 2-SLGT (slight), 3-ENH (enhanced), 4-MDT (moderate), 5-HIGH (high).
cards.ref: Aviation Weather Handbook (FAA-H-8083-28B) Section 27.16; NWS Storm Prediction Center

cards.question: What is a Center Weather Advisory (CWA), and what information does it contain?
cards.answer:
A CWA is an unscheduled, short-term weather advisory (a "nowcast") issued by the Center Weather Service Unit (CWSU) meteorologists at an ARTCC, mainly to help aircrews avoid adverse weather en route and in the terminal area.

A CWA is issued:
➢ To supplement an existing SIGMET, Convective SIGMET, or AIRMET
➢ When SIGMET/Convective SIGMET/AIRMET criteria are met or expected but no advisory has been issued yet
➢ When conditions do not meet advisory criteria but will still adversely affect the safe flow of air traffic

Contents: the phenomenon and its location (using VORs/reference points), height, extent, intensity, and movement. A CWA is valid for up to 2 hours and covers conditions beginning within 2 hours of issuance.
cards.ref: AIM 7-1-6; FAA Order JO 7110.10 Chapter 8 Section 8

cards.question: What is freezing level, what are some resources a pilot can use to find it, and how can a pilot estimate freezing level?
cards.answer:
The freezing level is the lowest altitude at which the air temperature is 0 °C. Above it, visible moisture can produce structural icing.

Resources:
➢ AWC Freezing Level analysis and forecast graphics (aviationweather.gov)
➢ GFA icing tab and G-AIRMET (freezing level is one of its depicted hazards)
➢ AIRMET Zulu text (includes freezing level heights)
➢ Winds and Temperatures Aloft (FB) forecast – find where temperatures cross 0 °C
➢ PIREPs and Skew-T soundings

Estimate: temperature decreases about 2 °C per 1,000 feet (standard lapse rate). Freezing level ≈ (surface temperature in °C ÷ 2) × 1,000 ft above the station. Example: 10 °C at the surface → freezing level about 5,000 ft AGL.
cards.ref: AIM 7-1-6; Aviation Weather Handbook (FAA-H-8083-28B) Sections 25.4 & 27.11; PHAK Chapter 12

cards.question: Describe why frost is a hazard to pilots, and what is the regulation regarding frost?
cards.answer:
Frost forms when the temperature of a surface is at or below the dew point and below freezing. Even a thin layer disrupts the airflow over the wing, which can drastically reduce lift and increase drag – the airplane may need a higher speed and longer roll to take off, may stall at a lower angle of attack, or may not become airborne at all.

Regulation: 14 CFR 91.527(a) states no pilot may take off an airplane with frost, ice, or snow adhering to any propeller, windshield, stabilizing or control surface, powerplant installation, airspeed/altimeter/rate-of-climb/attitude instrument system, or wing (frost under the wing in the area of the fuel tanks may be allowed if authorized by the FAA). 91.527 is in Part 91 Subpart F (large and turbine-powered multiengine airplanes); Parts 121 and 135 have similar clean-aircraft rules (e.g., 135.227).

For all aircraft, the FAA states an aircraft must be thoroughly cleaned and free of frost before beginning a flight.

cards.question: What is the relationship between temperature - dewpoint spread and cloud bases? What formula can be used to estimate cloud bases if temperature and dew point are known?
cards.answer:
As the temperature–dew point spread decreases, the air approaches saturation and cloud bases (or fog) get lower. When the spread reaches zero, moisture condenses into clouds or fog.

In a rising unsaturated parcel, the temperature drops about 5.4 °F per 1,000 ft and the dew point about 1 °F per 1,000 ft, so they converge at about 4.4 °F per 1,000 ft (≈2.5 °C).

Formula: (temperature – dew point) ÷ 4.4 × 1,000 = approximate cloud base in feet AGL.

Example: 85 °F temperature, 71 °F dew point → 14 ÷ 4.4 × 1,000 ≈ 3,180 ft AGL.

cards.question: Describe how ailerons work to control bank movement about the longitudinal axis.
cards.answer:
Ailerons are on the trailing edge of each wing and move in opposite directions. Moving the yoke/stick right raises the right aileron and lowers the left one.

The lowered aileron increases camber (and angle of attack) on that wing, producing more lift; the raised aileron decreases lift on its wing. The difference in lift rolls the airplane about the longitudinal axis toward the raised aileron.

Adverse yaw: the wing with the lowered aileron also produces more induced drag, yawing the nose away from the turn. Designs such as differential and Frise-type ailerons reduce, but do not eliminate, adverse yaw, so coordinated rudder is required.

cards.question: Describe how the rudder works to control yaw movement about the vertical axis.
cards.answer:
The rudder is attached to the back of the vertical stabilizer and is controlled by the rudder pedals. Pressing the left pedal deflects the rudder left, creating a sideways force on the tail that yaws the nose left about the vertical axis (and vice versa).

Rudder effectiveness increases with airspeed – large deflections are needed at slow speeds and small ones at high speeds. In propeller airplanes, slipstream flowing over the rudder increases its effectiveness at low speed.

The rudder is used to keep the airplane coordinated (counter adverse yaw and left-turning tendencies), not to turn the airplane.

cards.question: Describe how the elevator works to control pitch movement about the lateral axis.
cards.answer:
The elevator is attached to the back of the horizontal stabilizer. Pulling back on the yoke raises the elevator's trailing edge, increasing the downward aerodynamic force on the tail; the tail moves down and the nose pitches up about the lateral axis. Pushing forward does the opposite.

Some airplanes use a stabilator instead – a one-piece horizontal stabilizer that pivots from a central hinge point, usually with an antiservo tab to reduce sensitivity.

Elevator effectiveness depends on airspeed, power/propwash, and tail design (T-tails sit above propwash and wing downwash and may need more force at slow speeds).

cards.question: Describe the purpose of flaps and flap's affect on aerodynamics.
cards.answer:
Flaps are trailing-edge high-lift devices. Extending them increases camber (and on some types, wing area), which increases both lift and drag at a given angle of attack.

Effects:
➢ Lower stall speed and lower approach/landing speeds
➢ Steeper approach angle without increasing airspeed (added drag)
➢ Shorter takeoff/landing distances when used per the POH
➢ Pitch change when extended or retracted – usually trimmed out

Types: plain, split, slotted (most common), and Fowler (slides aft, increasing area and camber).

cards.question: Describe the basic components of a constant speed propeller and how the system functions.
cards.answer:
Components: propeller control (sets RPM), engine-driven governor, a hub with a pitch-change piston, and engine oil pressure (often boosted by a pump in the governor). Blade angle is moved one way by oil pressure and the other way by counterweights or the blades' centrifugal twisting moment, depending on the design.

Function: the pilot selects an RPM with the propeller control. The governor senses engine RPM and adjusts oil pressure to the hub, changing blade angle to keep that RPM constant:
➢ Airspeed increases (descent) → RPM tends to rise → governor increases blade angle
➢ Airspeed decreases (climb) → RPM tends to drop → governor decreases blade angle

The throttle controls power (shown on the manifold pressure gauge); the propeller control sets RPM (tachometer). To increase power, increase RPM first, then manifold pressure; to decrease power, reduce manifold pressure first, then RPM. If the blades reach a pitch stop, RPM varies like a fixed-pitch propeller.

cards.question: What is pre-ignition, how does it differ from detonation, and what are the dangers associated with it?
cards.answer:
Pre-ignition: the fuel-air mixture ignites before the normal spark-plug ignition event, usually from a hot spot in the cylinder (e.g., a glowing carbon deposit or a cracked spark plug insulator). The burning gases push against the piston while it is still rising on the compression stroke.

Detonation: the mixture ignites normally but then burns explosively (uncontrolled) instead of burning smoothly, causing excessive cylinder temperatures and pressures.

Danger: both cause high temperatures, loss of power, rough running, and severe engine damage (pistons, cylinders, valves) that can lead to engine failure. They often occur together and are hard to tell apart from the cockpit. Prevent them by using the correct fuel grade, enriching the mixture at high power, keeping CHTs in limits (cowl flaps open, shallow climbs), and avoiding high manifold pressure with low RPM.

cards.question: How does carburetor heat work on most aircraft?
cards.answer:
Carburetor heat routes heated air (typically from a shroud around the exhaust) into the induction system ahead of the carburetor instead of normal ram air. This keeps the fuel-air mixture above freezing to prevent carburetor ice, melts ice that has already formed, and provides an alternate air source if the intake filter becomes blocked.

Heated air is less dense, so the mixture becomes richer and power drops (up to about 15%).

Indications (fixed-pitch prop): applying carb heat causes an RPM drop. If ice is present, RPM then gradually rises as the ice melts; with no ice, RPM drops and stays constant. (Constant-speed prop: watch manifold pressure instead.)

cards.question: How does a magneto work? What does the magneto check conducted during a run up reveal to the pilot?
cards.answer:
A magneto is an engine-driven generator that uses a permanent magnet to produce high-voltage current for the spark plugs, completely independent of the airplane's electrical system. As long as the crankshaft turns, the magneto fires – the engine runs even with a dead battery/alternator.

Most engines have dual ignition: two magnetos, each firing one of the two spark plugs in every cylinder. This improves combustion and provides redundancy.

Run-up check (BOTH → R → BOTH → L → BOTH): expect a small RPM drop on each single magneto, within the POH limit and difference between mags.
➢ Normal drop – both ignition systems are working
➢ Excessive drop or rough running – fouled plugs, faulty wiring, or improper timing
➢ No drop – not normal; may indicate a broken magneto ground (P-lead), meaning that magneto may stay "hot" with the key off
➢ Engine quits on one magneto – do not fly

cards.question: What is unusable fuel?
cards.answer:
Unusable fuel is the fuel that remains in the tanks and lines that cannot be safely used by the engine in flight. The POH lists total and usable fuel; total – usable = unusable.

Unusable fuel is included in the airplane's empty weight (standard/basic and licensed empty weight), so it is already accounted for in weight and balance. Only usable fuel counts toward fuel load and fuel planning.

cards.question: Describe how a wet sump oil system works on general aviation aircraft.
cards.answer:
In a wet-sump system the oil is stored in a sump that is part of the engine.

➢ An engine-driven oil pump draws oil from the sump through a screen and pumps it under pressure through a filter (and oil cooler when hot) to the engine's bearings and moving parts
➢ A pressure relief valve returns excess oil to the sump to prevent over-pressurization
➢ After lubricating the engine, oil drains back to the sump by gravity; some parts are also lubricated by oil splashed by the crankshaft
➢ The oil level is checked with a dipstick at the filler cap

Oil lubricates, cools (carries heat away from cylinders), seals between piston rings and cylinder walls, and carries away contaminants. Monitor the oil pressure and oil temperature gauges.

cards.question: What is the difference between a circuit breaker and a fuse?
cards.answer:
Both protect electrical circuits and equipment from overload.

➢ Fuse – a wire element melts (blows) when current exceeds its rating and must be replaced. Spare fuses of the proper amperage should be carried; for night VFR, 91.205(c)(6) requires one spare set or three of each kind accessible to the pilot in flight.
➢ Circuit breaker – trips (pops) on overload and can be manually reset instead of replaced.

Follow the POH for resetting – generally reset a tripped breaker only once, and only if the equipment is needed.

cards.question: What are the different types of airspeeds?
cards.answer:
➢ Indicated Airspeed (IAS) – read directly from the airspeed indicator, uncorrected. POH V-speeds (stall, takeoff, landing) are in IAS.
➢ Calibrated Airspeed (CAS) – IAS corrected for instrument and installation (position) error. Error is greatest at low airspeeds.
➢ Equivalent Airspeed (EAS) – CAS corrected for air compressibility; significant mainly at high speeds and altitudes.
➢ True Airspeed (TAS) – CAS corrected for altitude and non-standard temperature; the actual speed through the air. Rule of thumb: TAS ≈ CAS + 2% per 1,000 ft.
➢ Groundspeed (GS) – TAS corrected for wind; the actual speed over the ground.

cards.question: What is an attitude heading reference system (AHRS) and how do modern glass avionic systems fail differently when compared to steam gauges?
cards.answer:
AHRS is a solid-state system that replaces the spinning gyros of traditional instruments. It uses solid-state rate sensors and accelerometers (and a magnetometer for heading) to provide attitude, heading, and slip/skid information to the primary flight display. Airspeed, altitude, and vertical speed come from a separate air data computer (ADC).

Failure differences:
➢ Steam gauges – a vacuum pump failure is often gradual and subtle: the gyros slowly spin down and the attitude/heading indicators drift and become inaccurate with no flag, so the pilot must catch it by cross-checking instruments and the suction gauge.
➢ Glass – AHRS/ADC failures are usually immediate and annunciated: the affected data is removed and typically replaced with a red X and an alert. An electrical failure can take out multiple displays at once, so the pilot must transition to standby instruments/backup display and the battery/standby power plan in the POH.

cards.question: What is the concept of a "sterile cockpit"?
cards.answer:
A sterile cockpit means no duties or activities other than those required for the safe operation of the aircraft during critical phases of flight – no non-essential conversation, eating, reading unrelated material, or company calls that could distract the crew.

Critical phases of flight are all ground operations involving taxi, takeoff and landing, and all other flight operations below 10,000 feet except cruise flight.

The rule is required for Part 121 and 135 crews, but it is a best practice for Part 91 pilots – brief passengers before flight not to talk during taxi, takeoff, approach, and landing, or when ATC is talking.

cards.question: What are the proper control positions for taxiing with different wind conditions and why?
cards.answer:
Hold the controls so that the wind cannot get under the upwind wing or tail:

➢ Quartering headwind – upwind aileron UP (turn the yoke into the wind) and elevator neutral (nosewheel airplane). The raised aileron reduces the wind's lifting effect on the upwind wing.
➢ Quartering tailwind – upwind aileron DOWN (turn the yoke away from the wind) and elevator DOWN (yoke forward). This keeps the wind from getting under the wing and tail and nosing over or lifting the airplane.

Memory aid: "climb into the wind, dive away from it." For strong headwinds in a tailwheel airplane, hold the elevator full up (yoke back).

cards.question: What is a runway incursion and when/where do they most commonly occur?
cards.answer:
A runway incursion is any occurrence at an airport involving the incorrect presence of an aircraft, vehicle, or person on the protected area of a surface designated for the landing and takeoff of aircraft.

Types: pilot deviations, operational incidents (ATC), and vehicle/pedestrian deviations. Pilot deviations are cited in more than 60% of incursions, and more than half involve general aviation (Part 91) operations.

Where/when they commonly occur:
➢ At runway holding position markings – crossing or entering a runway without a clearance
➢ At hot spots – complex or confusing taxiway/taxiway or taxiway/runway intersections
➢ While taxiing to the departure runway or back to the ramp after landing, especially at unfamiliar airports

Common causes: loss of situational awareness, distractions (heads-down, passengers), expectation bias with ATC instructions, and fatigue.
cards.ref: FAA Runway Safety – Runway Incursions; FAA GAJSC Runway Safety Topic (2014)

cards.question: How does a pilot control pilot-controlled lighting?
cards.answer:
Tune the CTAF or the published PCL frequency (Chart Supplement / sectional) and key the microphone:
➢ 7 times within 5 seconds – highest intensity available
➢ 5 times within 5 seconds – medium or lower intensity (lower REIL or REIL off)
➢ 3 times within 5 seconds – lowest intensity available (lower REIL or REIL off)

The lights stay on for 15 minutes from the most recent activation. The AIM suggests always keying 7 times first to ensure all controlled lights turn on at maximum intensity, then lowering the intensity if desired.

cards.question: Describe the differences in procedure for a short and soft field takeoff.
cards.answer:
Short-field takeoff – goal: shortest ground roll and steepest climb over an obstacle.
➢ Flaps per POH; start at the very beginning of the runway, aligned with the centerline
➢ Apply full power smoothly and without hesitation (some pilots hold the brakes until full power)
➢ Rotate at the POH speed and climb at VX until clear of obstacles (or 50 ft AGL), then accelerate to VY and retract flaps

Soft-field takeoff – goal: get the weight off the wheels as soon as possible.
➢ Flaps per POH; keep the airplane moving and taxi onto the runway without stopping
➢ Hold back pressure to raise the nosewheel and reduce its weight; lift off at the lowest possible airspeed
➢ Lower the nose and level off in ground effect to accelerate to VX or VY, then climb (VX if obstacles)
cards.ref: AFH Chapter 6; Private Pilot ACS PA.IV.C & PA.IV.E

cards.question: Describe the crosswind takeoff and landing technique.
cards.answer:
Crosswind takeoff:
➢ Start the roll with full aileron into the wind; reduce it as speed increases, keeping enough to hold the wings level
➢ Use rudder to keep the airplane tracking the centerline
➢ Hold the wheels on slightly longer, then make a smooth but definite liftoff to avoid side loads
➢ Once airborne, crab into the wind to maintain the extended centerline

Crosswind landing:
➢ Crab or wing-low (sideslip) method on final; the wing-low method is recommended in most cases
➢ Wing-low: aileron into the wind to stop drift, opposite rudder to keep the nose aligned with the runway
➢ Touch down on the upwind main wheel first while keeping the longitudinal axis aligned with the runway
➢ During rollout, keep increasing aileron into the wind as speed decreases – full aileron into the wind as the airplane comes to a stop

cards.question: What is a forward slip and when can a pilot use one? Are there any aircraft configuration restrictions for conducting forward slips?
cards.answer:
A forward slip is a way to increase the rate of descent without increasing airspeed. The pilot lowers one wing with aileron and applies opposite rudder so the nose yaws away from the low wing, while the airplane's flight path stays the same as before the slip. Power is normally at idle and pitch controls airspeed.

Uses: losing excess altitude on final approach (e.g., when high on approach or in airplanes without flaps) or for a forced landing.

Restrictions: check the AFM/POH – some airplanes have limitations or recommendations against slipping with flaps extended for aerodynamic reasons. Also expect the airspeed indicator to have significant error in a slip because of pitot/static port position.
cards.ref: AFH Chapter 9; Private Pilot ACS PA.IV.M

cards.question: What is the different between a forward and sideslip?
cards.answer:
Both use aileron and opposite rudder (cross-controlled); the difference is the purpose and where the nose points.

➢ Forward slip – used to lose altitude without gaining airspeed. The nose is yawed well away from the direction of travel, and the flight path stays the same as before the slip.
➢ Sideslip – used to correct for crosswind drift on landing. The wing is lowered into the wind with just enough opposite rudder to keep the nose aligned with the runway, so the airplane's longitudinal axis stays parallel to its flight path while it moves sideways toward the low wing to cancel drift.

cards.question: Normal Takeoff and Climb (PA.IV.A): What are the ACS tolerances?
cards.answer:
Rotate and lift off at the recommended airspeed and accelerate to VY, then pitch for VY (or the manufacturer's recommended climb speed) +10/-5 knots and maintain VY +10/-5 knots to a safe maneuvering altitude.

Also: confirm takeoff power and engine indications before rotation, configure the airplane after a positive rate of climb (or per the POH/AFM), maintain directional control and wind-drift correction throughout, verify the assigned/correct runway, and comply with noise abatement procedures.
cards.ref: Private Pilot ACS PA.IV.A; AFH Chapter 6

cards.question: Normal Approach and Landing (PA.IV.B): What are the ACS tolerances?
cards.answer:
Approach at the recommended speed, or if none, not more than 1.3 VSO, +10/-5 knots with gust factor applied. Touch down at a proper pitch attitude within 400 feet beyond or on the specified point, with no side drift and the longitudinal axis aligned with the runway centerline.

Also: maintain a stabilized approach and crosswind correction, make smooth round-out and touchdown, and execute a timely go-around if the approach or landing cannot be made safely.
cards.ref: Private Pilot ACS PA.IV.B; AFH Chapter 9

cards.question: Soft-Field Takeoff and Climb (PA.IV.C): What are the ACS standards?
cards.answer:
Taxi onto the takeoff surface without stopping while smoothly advancing to takeoff power; hold a pitch attitude that transfers weight from the wheels to the wings as quickly as possible; lift off at the lowest possible airspeed and stay in ground effect while accelerating to VX or VY; then climb at VX or VY +10/-5 knots.

Configure the airplane after a positive rate of climb, and maintain directional control and wind-drift correction throughout.
cards.ref: Private Pilot ACS PA.IV.C; AFH Chapter 6

cards.question: Soft-Field Approach and Landing (PA.IV.D): What are the ACS standards?
cards.answer:
Approach at the recommended speed, or if none, not more than 1.3 VSO, +10/-5 knots with gust factor applied. Touch down at a proper pitch attitude with minimum sink rate, no side drift, and the longitudinal axis aligned with the runway centerline (there is no touchdown-point distance tolerance).

Keep the nosewheel off the surface until elevator effectiveness is lost, maintain elevator control during rollout, and keep enough speed to exit the soft area without sinking in.
cards.ref: Private Pilot ACS PA.IV.D; AFH Chapter 9

cards.question: Short-Field Takeoff and Maximum Performance Climb (PA.IV.E): What are the ACS tolerances?
cards.answer:
Use the maximum available takeoff area, hold brakes while setting maximum-performance power, and confirm takeoff power before brake release. Rotate at the recommended speed and accelerate to the obstacle clearance speed or VX +10/-5 knots, holding it until the obstacle is cleared or 50 feet above the surface. Then pitch for VY +10/-5 knots and maintain VY +10/-5 knots to a safe maneuvering altitude.

Configure the airplane after a positive rate of climb and maintain directional control and drift correction.
cards.ref: Private Pilot ACS PA.IV.E; AFH Chapter 6

cards.question: Short-Field Approach and Landing (PA.IV.F): What are the ACS tolerances?
cards.answer:
Approach at the recommended speed, or if none, not more than 1.3 VSO, +10/-5 knots with gust factor applied. Touch down at a proper pitch attitude within 200 feet beyond or on the specified point, with no side drift, minimum float, and the longitudinal axis aligned with the runway centerline.

Use the manufacturer's recommended configuration and braking after touchdown.
cards.ref: Private Pilot ACS PA.IV.F; AFH Chapter 9

cards.question: Forward Slip to a Landing (PA.IV.M): What are the ACS standards?
cards.answer:
Touch down at a proper pitch attitude within 400 feet beyond or on the specified point, with no side drift and the longitudinal axis aligned with the runway centerline, while keeping the ground track aligned with the runway centerline.

Position on a downwind leg parallel to the landing runway, configure correctly, and (if there's a crosswind) slip into the wind and transition to a sideslip before touchdown.
cards.ref: Private Pilot ACS PA.IV.M; AFH Chapter 9

cards.question: Go-Around/Rejected Landing (PA.IV.N): What are the ACS tolerances?
cards.answer:
Make a timely decision to go around, apply takeoff power immediately, and pitch for VX or VY as appropriate +10/-5 knots. Configure after a positive rate of climb (or per the manufacturer), then maintain VY +10/-5 knots to a safe maneuvering altitude.

Move to the side of the runway if needed to see and avoid conflicting traffic, and maintain directional control and wind-drift correction throughout the climb.
cards.ref: Private Pilot ACS PA.IV.N; AFH Chapter 9

cards.question: Steep Turns (PA.V.A): What are the ACS tolerances?
cards.answer:
Enter at the manufacturer's recommended speed (or not more than VA) and roll into a coordinated 360° turn at about 45° bank, then do the same in the opposite direction if the evaluator asks. Maintain entry altitude ±100 feet, airspeed ±10 knots, bank ±5°, and roll out on the entry heading ±10°.

At 45° bank the load factor is about 1.4 G, so stall speed rises about 19%. Add back pressure (and power as needed) to hold altitude, and counter the overbanking tendency.
cards.ref: Private Pilot ACS PA.V.A; AFH Chapter 10

cards.question: Ground Reference Maneuvers (PA.V.B): Which maneuvers can be tested, and what are the ACS tolerances?
cards.answer:
The evaluator selects at least one of: rectangular course, S-turns, or turns around a point. Enter at 600 to 1,000 feet AGL and maintain altitude ±100 feet and airspeed ±10 knots.

Apply wind-drift correction to hold a constant ground track (rectangular course) or a constant radius (S-turns, turns around a point). Divide your attention between airplane control, traffic, and the ground track while staying coordinated.
cards.ref: Private Pilot ACS PA.V.B; AFH Chapter 7

cards.question: Rectangular Course: How is it entered, and where is the steepest bank?
cards.answer:
Enter at 600 to 1,000 feet AGL, 45° to the downwind leg, at a suitable distance from the reference area (left or right pattern). Hold altitude ±100 feet and airspeed ±10 knots.

The steepest bank is in the turn from downwind to base (highest groundspeed). The shallowest bank is in the turn from upwind to crosswind (lowest groundspeed). Crab into the wind on each leg to keep the ground track parallel to the field boundaries.
cards.ref: Private Pilot ACS PA.V.B.S3a; AFH Chapter 7

cards.question: S-Turns: How are they entered, and how is bank varied?
cards.answer:
Enter perpendicular to the reference line at 600 to 1,000 feet AGL, normally downwind. Fly a series of equal-radius semicircles on each side of the line, reversing the turn directly over the line. Hold altitude ±100 feet and airspeed ±10 knots.

The bank is steepest when headed downwind (highest groundspeed) and shallowest when headed upwind, so that each half-circle has a constant radius.
cards.ref: Private Pilot ACS PA.V.B.S3b; AFH Chapter 7

cards.question: Turns Around a Point: How is it entered, and where is the steepest bank?
cards.answer:
Enter at 600 to 1,000 feet AGL at a suitable distance from the point (normally on a downwind entry) and complete turns in either direction as the evaluator specifies. Hold altitude ±100 feet and airspeed ±10 knots.

The bank is steepest when headed directly downwind (highest groundspeed) and shallowest when headed directly upwind (lowest groundspeed), so the radius around the point stays constant.
cards.ref: Private Pilot ACS PA.V.B.S3c; AFH Chapter 7

cards.question: Maneuvering During Slow Flight (PA.VII.A): What are the ACS tolerances?
cards.answer:
Choose an entry altitude that lets you finish no lower than 1,500 feet AGL. Fly at a speed where any further increase in angle of attack or load factor, or any reduction in power, would cause a stall warning. Maintain the specified altitude ±100 feet, heading ±10°, airspeed +10/-0 knots, and bank angle ±10°.

Perform coordinated straight-and-level flight, turns, climbs, and descents in the configurations the evaluator specifies, without triggering a stall warning.
cards.ref: Private Pilot ACS PA.VII.A; AFH Chapter 5

cards.question: Power-Off Stalls (PA.VII.B): What are the ACS standards?
cards.answer:
Choose an entry altitude that lets you recover no lower than 1,500 feet AGL. Set the approach or landing configuration and establish a stabilized descent. Maintain heading ±10° in straight flight, or a bank of no more than 20° ±10° in turning flight. Acknowledge the cues of the impending stall, then recover promptly after a full stall occurs.

Recover per the POH/AFM (reduce angle of attack, level the wings, add power). Configure as recommended, accelerate to VX or VY, and return to the altitude, heading, and airspeed the evaluator specifies.
cards.ref: Private Pilot ACS PA.VII.B; AFH Chapter 5

cards.question: Power-On Stalls (PA.VII.C): What are the ACS standards?
cards.answer:
Choose an entry altitude that lets you recover no lower than 1,500 feet AGL. Use the takeoff, departure, or cruise configuration the evaluator specifies, with power set to no less than 65%. Maintain heading ±10° in straight flight, or a bank of no more than 20° ±10° in turning flight. Acknowledge the cues of the impending stall, then recover promptly after a full stall occurs.

Recover per the POH/AFM. Configure as recommended, accelerate to VX or VY, and return to the altitude, heading, and airspeed the evaluator specifies.
cards.ref: Private Pilot ACS PA.VII.C; AFH Chapter 5

cards.question: Basic Instrument Maneuvers – Straight-and-Level Flight (PA.VIII.A): What are the ACS tolerances?
cards.answer:
Maintain altitude ±200 feet, heading ±20°, and airspeed ±10 knots, solely by reference to instruments.

Use a proper instrument cross-check and interpretation, with coordinated control inputs.
cards.ref: Private Pilot ACS PA.VIII.A; Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15)

cards.question: Basic Instrument Maneuvers – Constant Airspeed Climbs (PA.VIII.B): What are the ACS tolerances?
cards.answer: Transition to the climb pitch attitude and power setting on an assigned heading, and climb at a constant airspeed to specified altitudes in straight flight and turns. Level off at the assigned altitude and maintain altitude ±200 feet, heading ±20°, and airspeed ±10 knots.
cards.ref: Private Pilot ACS PA.VIII.B; Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15)

cards.question: Basic Instrument Maneuvers – Constant Airspeed Descents (PA.VIII.C): What are the ACS tolerances?
cards.answer: Transition to the descent pitch attitude and power setting on an assigned heading, and descend at a constant airspeed to specified altitudes in straight flight and turns. Level off at the assigned altitude and maintain altitude ±200 feet, heading ±20°, and airspeed ±10 knots.
cards.ref: Private Pilot ACS PA.VIII.C; Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15)

cards.question: Basic Instrument Maneuvers – Turns to Headings (PA.VIII.D): What are the ACS tolerances?
cards.answer: Use a standard-rate turn (3° per second) to the assigned heading. Maintain altitude ±200 feet and airspeed ±10 knots, and roll out on the assigned heading ±10°.
cards.ref: Private Pilot ACS PA.VIII.D; Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15)

cards.question: Recovery from Unusual Flight Attitudes (PA.VIII.E): What is the ACS standard, and what is the recovery sequence?
cards.answer:
Using instruments only, identify the unusual attitude (nose-high or nose-low) and apply the correct control, power, and configuration inputs in the correct sequence to return to stabilized level flight. There is no numeric tolerance; the recovery must be prompt, coordinated, and smooth.

Nose-high (airspeed decreasing): add power, lower the nose, level the wings.
Nose-low (airspeed increasing): reduce power, level the wings, then raise the nose to level flight.
cards.ref: Private Pilot ACS PA.VIII.E; Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15)

cards.question: Emergency Descent (PA.IX.A): What are the ACS tolerances?
cards.answer:
Use a bank angle between 30° and 45° to keep positive load factors during the descent. Maintain the appropriate descent airspeed +0/-10 knots, and level off at the specified altitude ±100 feet.

Establish the airspeed and configuration the POH/AFM recommends, stay oriented, plan a smooth recovery, and complete the appropriate checklist(s) and radio calls.
cards.ref: Private Pilot ACS PA.IX.A; AFH Chapter 18

cards.question: Emergency Approach and Landing (Simulated) (PA.IX.B): What are the ACS standards?
cards.answer:
Establish and maintain the recommended best glide airspeed ±10 knots.

Configure the airplane per the POH/AFM, select a suitable landing area (considering altitude, wind, terrain, obstructions, and glide distance), plan and follow a flightpath to it, prepare for landing as the evaluator specifies, and complete the appropriate checklist(s).
cards.ref: Private Pilot ACS PA.IX.B; AFH Chapter 18

cards.question: When must a pilot hold an instrument rating to act as pilot in command?
cards.answer:
➢ Any flight under IFR, or in weather conditions below VFR minimums (14 CFR 61.3(e)).
➢ Any flight in Class A airspace, since all operations there are IFR (14 CFR 91.135).
➢ Special VFR at night (between sunset and sunrise): the pilot must meet the Part 61 instrument requirements and the aircraft must be IFR-equipped per 91.205(d) (14 CFR 91.157(b)(4)).
➢ Commercial pilots: without an instrument rating, the certificate is limited to no carriage of passengers for hire on cross-country flights of more than 50 NM or at night (14 CFR 61.133(b)).

cards.question: What instrument experience is required to act as PIC under IFR, and what happens if it lapses?
cards.answer:
Within the 6 calendar months before the month of the flight, perform and log ("6 HIT"):
➢ 6 instrument approaches
➢ Holding procedures and tasks
➢ Intercepting and Tracking courses using navigation systems

These may be done in actual conditions or with a view-limiting device (with a safety pilot), or in a full flight simulator, FTD, or ATD representing the aircraft category. No instructor is required.

If currency lapses, the pilot has the next 6 calendar months to complete the tasks with a safety pilot, instructor, or in a device. After that 6-month grace period, only an Instrument Proficiency Check (IPC) restores currency.

cards.question: What is an Instrument Proficiency Check (IPC), who may give one, and when is it required?
cards.answer:
An IPC is required when a pilot has not met the 6-month instrument experience requirement for more than 6 calendar months (i.e., beyond the grace period).

➢ Content: the areas of operation in the Instrument Rating ACS (Part 61 Appendix A) appropriate to the rating.
➢ Where: in an aircraft of the appropriate category, or in a full flight simulator/FTD representative of that category.
➢ Who: an examiner, an authorized instructor (CFII), a qualifying company check pilot, an Armed Forces instrument check pilot (for members), or a person approved by the FAA.

cards.question: When may a pilot log instrument time, and what must be recorded to use it for instrument currency?
cards.answer:
➢ Instrument time may be logged only when the pilot operates the aircraft solely by reference to instruments, in actual or simulated instrument conditions.
➢ An authorized instructor may log instrument time when giving instrument instruction in actual instrument conditions.

For 61.57(c) currency, the logbook must show:
➢ The location and type of each instrument approach
➢ The name of the safety pilot, if one was required

Simulator/FTD/ATD time: for a certificate or rating, an authorized instructor must be present and sign; for recency, the record must show the device, time, and content.

cards.question: What are the requirements to fly in simulated instrument conditions with a safety pilot?
cards.answer:
➢ The other control seat must be occupied by a safety pilot holding at least a private pilot certificate with category and class ratings appropriate to the aircraft.
➢ The safety pilot must have adequate vision forward and to each side (or a competent observer must supplement it).
➢ The aircraft must have fully functioning dual controls (a single throwover control wheel is allowed in some single-engine airplanes if the safety pilot determines the flight can be conducted safely and the pilot flying holds at least a private certificate).

Because the safety pilot is a required flight crewmember for the flight, they should also hold a current medical certificate (or be operating under BasicMed). The safety pilot does not need to be instrument rated or current.

cards.question: What instruments and equipment are required for IFR flight?
cards.answer:
All day VFR equipment (plus night VFR equipment at night), and "GRABCARD":
➢ G - Generator or alternator of adequate capacity
➢ R - Radios: two-way communication and navigation equipment suitable for the route
➢ A - Altimeter, sensitive and adjustable for barometric pressure
➢ B - Ball (slip-skid indicator)
➢ C - Clock showing hours, minutes, and seconds with a sweep-second pointer or digital presentation
➢ A - Attitude indicator (gyroscopic pitch and bank)
➢ R - Rate-of-turn indicator (gyroscopic)
➢ D - Directional gyro (heading indicator or equivalent)

At or above FL 240, if VOR navigation is required, DME or a suitable RNAV system is also required.

cards.question: What are the fuel requirements for flight in IFR conditions (airplanes)?
cards.answer:
Enough fuel, considering weather reports and forecasts, to:
➢ Fly to the first airport of intended landing
➢ Then fly to the alternate airport (if an alternate is required)
➢ Then fly for 45 minutes at normal cruising speed

Compare VFR: 30 minutes reserve by day, 45 minutes at night (14 CFR 91.151).

cards.question: When is an alternate airport required on an IFR flight plan (airplanes)?
cards.answer:
An alternate is required unless BOTH are true:
➢ The destination has a published (Part 97) or approved special instrument approach procedure, AND
➢ Weather reports/forecasts show that from 1 hour before to 1 hour after the ETA, the ceiling will be at least 2,000 ft above airport elevation and visibility at least 3 SM.

Memory aid: the "1-2-3 rule" (1 hour either side, 2,000 ft ceiling, 3 SM visibility).

cards.question: What weather must be forecast at an airport for it to be listed as an IFR alternate (airplanes)?
cards.answer:
At the ETA at the alternate:
➢ If the airport has an instrument approach: the alternate minimums published for that procedure, or if none are published, the standard minimums:
   - Precision approach: 600 ft ceiling and 2 SM visibility
   - Nonprecision approach: 800 ft ceiling and 2 SM visibility
➢ If the airport has no instrument approach: ceiling and visibility that allow descent from the MEA, approach, and landing under basic VFR.

Check the approach chart for the ▲A symbol, which means nonstandard alternate minimums apply or the airport is not authorized as an alternate.

cards.question: What reports are required by regulation when operating under IFR in controlled airspace?
cards.answer:
The PIC must maintain a continuous listening watch on the appropriate frequency and report as soon as possible:
➢ The time and altitude of passing each designated (compulsory) reporting point, or points specified by ATC. Under radar control, only points ATC specifically requests
➢ Any unforecast weather conditions encountered
➢ Any other information relating to the safety of flight

Also, any malfunction of navigation, approach, or communication equipment in controlled airspace must be reported (14 CFR 91.187).

cards.question: Besides the regulatory reports, what additional reports should an IFR pilot make to ATC without being asked?
cards.answer:
At all times:
➢ Vacating any previously assigned altitude for a newly assigned altitude
➢ Making an altitude change on a VFR-on-top clearance
➢ Unable to climb or descend at least 500 fpm
➢ Missed approach (request clearance for specific action)
➢ True airspeed at cruise changes by 5% or 10 knots (whichever is greater) from the flight plan
➢ Time and altitude on reaching a holding fix or clearance limit, and when leaving a holding fix
➢ Loss of VOR, TACAN, ADF, GPS (anomalies), ILS, or communications capability in controlled airspace
➢ Any information relating to safety of flight

When not in radar contact (in addition):
➢ Leaving the final approach fix inbound on a nonprecision approach (or the outer marker)
➢ A corrected estimate when a previously submitted estimate is in error by more than 2 minutes (3 minutes or more in North Atlantic airspace)

cards.question: When does 14 CFR 91.21 restrict the use of portable electronic devices (PEDs), and which PEDs are always allowed?
cards.answer:
91.21 applies to:
➢ Aircraft operated by holders of an air carrier or operating certificate (Part 121/135 etc.)
➢ Any other U.S.-registered civil aircraft while operated under IFR

Always allowed: portable voice recorders, hearing aids, heart pacemakers, electric shavers.

Any other PED is allowed if the operator determines it will not interfere with the aircraft's navigation or communication systems. For Part 91 aircraft, the PIC or other operator may make that determination; for certificate holders, the operator must.

cards.question: What do ATC light gun signals mean for an aircraft on the ground and an aircraft in flight?
cards.answer:
➢ Steady green: Ground - cleared for takeoff | Air - cleared to land
➢ Flashing green: Ground - cleared to taxi | Air - return for landing (followed by steady green at the proper time)
➢ Steady red: Ground - stop | Air - give way to other aircraft and continue circling
➢ Flashing red: Ground - taxi clear of the runway in use | Air - airport unsafe, do not land
➢ Flashing white: Ground - return to starting point on airport | Air - not applicable
➢ Alternating red and green: Ground and Air - exercise extreme caution

cards.question: What does 14 CFR 91.107 require of the PIC regarding safety belts, shoulder harnesses, and child restraints?
cards.answer:
➢ Before takeoff: brief each person on how to fasten and unfasten their safety belt and, if installed, shoulder harness.
➢ Before moving on the surface, takeoff, and landing: ensure each person has been notified to fasten their belt and harness.
➢ During surface movement, takeoff, and landing: each person must occupy an approved seat or berth with belt (and harness, if installed) secured.

Exceptions include:
➢ A child who has not reached their second birthday may be held by an adult occupying an approved seat
➢ Sport parachutists may use the floor as a seat
➢ A child may use an approved child restraint system (properly labeled) if accompanied by a parent, guardian, or designated attendant

cards.question: Which operations are excepted from the ELT requirement, and when must ELT batteries be replaced?
cards.answer:
Common exceptions to the ELT requirement:
➢ Training operations conducted entirely within a 50 NM radius of the airport where the local flight began
➢ Flight operations incident to design and testing, or to the manufacture, preparation, and delivery of new aircraft
➢ Aerial application of chemicals for agricultural purposes
➢ Aircraft equipped to carry not more than one person
➢ Scheduled flights by scheduled air carriers
➢ Research and development, exhibition, air racing, market surveys, crew training
➢ ELT temporarily removed for maintenance: allowed up to 90 days with a logbook entry and an "ELT not installed" placard
➢ Ferrying a newly acquired airplane, or one with an inoperative ELT, to a place where it can be installed or repaired

Battery replacement (or recharge): after more than 1 cumulative hour of use, or when 50% of the battery's useful life (or charge life) has expired.

cards.question: How does a pilot request an ATC deviation from the transponder requirements?
cards.answer:
Requests go to the ATC facility having jurisdiction over the airspace:
➢ Transponder working but no Mode C (altitude reporting): request may be made at any time
➢ Inoperative transponder, to fly to the destination (including intermediate stops) or to a repair facility: request may be made at any time
➢ Aircraft not equipped with a transponder: request must be made at least 1 hour before the proposed operation

cards.question: What is the "truth-in-leasing" requirement and when does it apply?
cards.answer:
It applies to leases and conditional sales contracts of U.S.-registered LARGE civil aircraft (over 12,500 lb). The lease must be in writing and include a large-print truth-in-leasing clause, just above the signatures, stating:
➢ The regulations under which the aircraft was maintained and inspected during the preceding 12 months, and its compliance status for the intended operation
➢ The name, address, and signature of the person responsible for operational control, and certification that each party understands its responsibilities
➢ That an explanation of operational control can be obtained from the responsible Flight Standards office

Before operating: mail a copy to the FAA Aircraft Registration Branch within 24 hours of execution, carry a copy aboard, and notify the responsible Flight Standards office at least 48 hours before the first flight under the lease.

Why it matters: it makes clear who holds operational control, preventing illegal charter disguised as a lease.

cards.question: What is the NTSB definition of an aircraft accident versus an incident?
cards.answer:
➢ Aircraft accident: an occurrence associated with the operation of an aircraft, between the time any person boards with the intention of flight and all persons have disembarked, in which any person suffers death or serious injury, or the aircraft receives substantial damage.
➢ Incident: an occurrence other than an accident, associated with the operation of an aircraft, which affects or could affect the safety of operations.

A fatal injury is one that results in death within 30 days of the accident.

cards.question: How does the NTSB define "serious injury" and "substantial damage"?
cards.answer:
Serious injury - any injury which:
➢ Requires hospitalization for more than 48 hours, starting within 7 days of the injury
➢ Fractures any bone (except simple fractures of fingers, toes, or nose)
➢ Causes severe hemorrhages, or nerve, muscle, or tendon damage
➢ Involves any internal organ
➢ Involves second- or third-degree burns, or any burns affecting more than 5% of the body surface

Substantial damage - damage or failure that adversely affects structural strength, performance, or flight characteristics and would normally require major repair or replacement of the component.

NOT substantial damage: engine failure or damage limited to one engine, bent fairings or cowling, dented skin, small punctures in skin or fabric, ground damage to propeller or rotor blades, and damage to landing gear, wheels, tires, flaps, engine accessories, brakes, or wingtips.

cards.question: When must the operator immediately notify the NTSB?
cards.answer:
Immediately, by the most expeditious means, for an accident or any of these serious incidents:
➢ Flight control system malfunction or failure
➢ Inability of a required flight crewmember to perform duties due to injury or illness
➢ Failure of an internal turbine engine component with debris escaping other than out the exhaust path
➢ In-flight fire
➢ Aircraft collision in flight
➢ Damage to property other than the aircraft estimated to exceed $25,000
➢ Release of all or part of a propeller blade (other than from ground contact)
➢ Complete loss of information (excluding flickering) from more than 50% of the EFIS/EICAS/ECAM-type cockpit displays
➢ An ACAS resolution advisory on an IFR flight plan that is needed to avoid a substantial risk of collision
➢ Certain large multiengine aircraft (>12,500 lb) system failures, and certain air carrier runway events
➢ An overdue aircraft believed to have been in an accident

cards.question: After an accident or incident, what must the operator preserve, and when must a written report be filed?
cards.answer:
➢ Preserve the wreckage, cargo, mail, and all records (including flight, maintenance, and voice recorders) until the NTSB takes custody or releases them. Wreckage may be moved only to remove injured or trapped persons, protect it from further damage, or protect the public.
➢ File NTSB Form 6120.1 within 10 days after an accident, or after 7 days if an overdue aircraft is still missing.
➢ For an incident requiring immediate notification, a report is filed only if the NTSB requests it.
➢ Each crewmember, if physically able, attaches a statement of the facts.

cards.question: What do the colors of an airport rotating beacon indicate, and what can a daytime beacon mean?
cards.answer:
➢ White and green: lighted land airport
➢ White and yellow: lighted water airport
➢ Green, yellow, and white: lighted heliport
➢ Military airport: alternating white and green, with two quick white flashes between the green flashes
(Green alone or yellow alone is used only together with a white-green or white-yellow display.)

In Class B, C, D, and E surface areas, a beacon operating during daylight often indicates ground visibility below 3 miles and/or ceiling below 1,000 ft, so an ATC clearance is required. Don't rely on the beacon alone; there is no regulatory requirement for daytime operation.

cards.question: What colors are taxiway edge lights, taxiway centerline lights, and runway end identifier lights (REIL)?
cards.answer:
➢ Taxiway edge lights: blue
➢ Taxiway centerline lights: steady green
➢ REIL: a pair of synchronized flashing lights, one on each side of the runway threshold. They give quick, positive identification of the approach end of a runway surrounded by other lights, lacking contrast with terrain, or in reduced visibility.

cards.question: How are airframe icing intensities (trace, light, moderate, severe) defined for PIREPs?
cards.answer:
➢ Trace: ice becomes noticeable; accumulation slightly greater than sublimation (reference: under 1/4 inch per hour). Consider exiting.
➢ Light: requires occasional cycling of manual deicing systems (reference: 1/4 to 1 inch per hour). Consider exiting.
➢ Moderate: requires frequent cycling of manual deicing systems (reference: 1 to 3 inches per hour). Exit as soon as possible.
➢ Severe: ice protection systems fail to remove the accumulation, and ice forms in areas not normally prone to icing (reference: more than 3 inches per hour). Immediate exit is required.

Severity is aircraft dependent. Include aircraft type when reporting icing.

cards.question: In a METAR remarks section, what do AO1/AO2, SLP, and the T-group (e.g., T01820159) mean?
cards.answer:
➢ AO1: automated station without a precipitation discriminator
➢ AO2: automated station with a precipitation discriminator (can tell liquid from frozen precipitation)
➢ SLP045: sea-level pressure in hectopascals to the tenth; add a leading 10 or 9 (whichever gives a value closest to 1000) - here 1004.5 hPa
➢ T01820159: temperature and dew point to the tenth of a degree C. The first digit of each 4-digit group is the sign (0 = positive, 1 = negative): temperature 18.2°C, dew point 15.9°C

cards.question: What are the different types (functions) of Class E airspace?
cards.answer:
➢ Surface areas: for airports without an operating control tower (or part-time C/D towers), from the surface up; dashed magenta on sectionals
➢ Extensions to surface areas: begin at the surface to contain instrument approaches without imposing a VFR communications requirement
➢ Transition areas: begin at 700 ft AGL (magenta vignette) or 1,200 ft AGL (blue vignette) for airports with instrument procedures
➢ En route domestic areas: controlled airspace where IFR en route service is needed but airways are inadequate
➢ Federal airways and low-altitude RNAV (T) routes: generally 1,200 ft AGL up to but not including 18,000 ft MSL
➢ Offshore airspace areas: up to but not including 18,000 ft MSL
➢ Unless designated lower, Class E begins at 14,500 ft MSL; all airspace above FL 600 is Class E

cards.question: What are VFR waypoints, and how are they used?
cards.answer:
VFR waypoints supplement visual navigation for aircraft with area navigation (GPS) receivers, e.g., around Class B/C airspace, Special Use Airspace, and mountain passes.

➢ Names are five letters beginning with "VP" and are retrievable from the navigation database
➢ Stand-alone VFR waypoints use the four-point star symbol; those collocated with visual checkpoints are shown with a magenta flag
➢ "VP" names are not for use in ATC communications; collocated visual checkpoint names may be used
➢ Usable on VFR flight plans and only under VFR conditions; not accepted on IFR flight plans
➢ They do not relieve the pilot of any Part 91 requirements; current VFR charts remain the primary reference

cards.question: What is the difference between RNAV and RNP?
cards.answer:
➢ RNAV (area navigation): a method of navigation that allows operation on any desired flight path within coverage of navigation aids or self-contained systems, rather than only between ground-based NAVAIDs. GPS is the most common RNAV system.
➢ RNP (required navigation performance): RNAV with the added requirement for onboard performance monitoring and alerting (OBPMA) - the system monitors its own accuracy and alerts the pilot if the required performance is not being met.

Check the AFM/avionics documents for the aircraft's RNP eligibility.

cards.question: If the fuel grade specified for your engine is not available, what may you use?
cards.answer:
Use the next higher grade as a substitute. Never use a lower grade than recommended - it can push cylinder head and oil temperatures beyond their normal ranges and may cause detonation.

Automobile gasoline may be used only if the aircraft has been approved for it by a Supplemental Type Certificate (STC). The proper grade is in the AFM/POH, on flight deck placards, and next to the filler caps.

cards.question: How do you interpret an ammeter, and what do full-scale deflections indicate?
cards.answer:
The ammeter (zero at center) shows whether the alternator/generator is supplying adequate power and whether the battery is charging.
➢ Plus (+) side: charging rate of the battery
➢ Minus (-) side: more current is being drawn from the battery than is being replaced
➢ Full-scale minus deflection: alternator/generator malfunction
➢ Full-scale positive deflection: voltage regulator malfunction

In either case, follow the AFM/POH. Some aircraft use a loadmeter (shows load on the alternator) or a low-voltage warning light instead.

cards.question: What is the difference between anti-ice and deice equipment, and what types are common?
cards.answer:
➢ Anti-ice: prevents ice from forming.
➢ Deice: removes ice after it has formed.

Common systems:
➢ Pneumatic deicing boots on wing/tail leading edges, inflated to crack off ice (can be cycled as soon as ice is observed - modern boots don't "bridge")
➢ Thermal anti-ice (heated leading edges, e.g., engine bleed air)
➢ Weeping-wing (TKS) fluid systems
➢ Electrically heated propeller boots or fluid prop anti-ice
➢ Windshield anti-ice (heat or fluid)
➢ Heated pitot tubes, static ports, fuel vents, and stall-warning sensors

Most light aircraft have only pitot heat and are not certified for flight in icing; they must exit icing immediately.

cards.question: What types of supplemental oxygen systems are used in aircraft, and why must aviator's breathing oxygen be used?
cards.answer:
➢ Continuous-flow: common for passengers; mask with a reservoir bag that collects oxygen while the user exhales
➢ Diluter-demand: supplies oxygen only on inhalation, mixed with cabin air based on altitude
➢ Pressure-demand: like diluter-demand but supplies oxygen under positive pressure above about 34,000 ft cabin altitude; safe above 40,000 ft
➢ Electrical pulse-demand (portable): delivers oxygen at the start of each inhalation, conserving supply

Containers should be filled with oxygen that meets the Aviator's Breathing Oxygen purity standard (SAE AS8010), and the system should be inspected and serviced periodically.

cards.question: How does a typical cabin pressurization system work?
cards.answer:
➢ The cabin, flight deck, and baggage compartments form a sealed unit holding air at higher pressure than outside.
➢ Air comes from turbine engine bleed air, or on piston aircraft from turbochargers through a sonic venturi (flow limiter).
➢ An outflow valve releases air; regulating it controls cabin pressure while allowing constant fresh-air flow.
➢ A typical system holds about an 8,000 ft cabin altitude at the airplane's maximum design cruising altitude.

Key instruments/controls: cabin altimeter, cabin rate-of-climb indicator, differential pressure gauge, cabin pressure controller, safety (relief) valve, and dump valve.

cards.question: What happens to the pitot-static instruments when the alternate static source (inside the cabin) is used?
cards.answer:
Cabin pressure is slightly lower than outside static pressure (venturi effect around the fuselage), so:
➢ Altimeter: indicates slightly higher than actual
➢ Airspeed indicator: indicates greater than actual
➢ VSI: shows a momentary climb, then stabilizes if altitude is held

Check the AFM/POH for correction values. With no alternate source, breaking the VSI glass vents static pressure to the other instruments (sacrificing the VSI).

cards.question: How do you calculate the new CG after shifting weight within the aircraft?
cards.answer:
Use the weight-shift proportion:

Weight shifted ÷ Total weight = Change in CG ÷ Distance weight is moved

Example: a 2,400 lb airplane with CG at 40.0 in moves 60 lb of baggage from station 37 to station 95 (58 in aft).
ΔCG = 60 × 58 ÷ 2,400 = 1.45 in → new CG = 41.45 in (moved aft).

Alternatively: new total moment ÷ total weight. Moving weight aft increases total moment; forward decreases it. Total weight does not change.

cards.question: What three conditions are required for a thunderstorm to form?
cards.answer:
➢ Sufficient water vapor (moisture)
➢ An unstable lapse rate
➢ An initial lifting action (e.g., surface heating, fronts, terrain, converging winds)

Air mass thunderstorms come mainly from surface heating and are usually short-lived; steady-state thunderstorms are forced by weather systems (fronts, troughs) and can form squall lines.

cards.question: What are autokinesis and the false horizon illusion, and how can you prevent them?
cards.answer:
➢ Autokinesis: staring at a single point of light against a dark background for more than a few seconds (movement begins in about 8-10 seconds) makes the light appear to move. Prevent it by scanning, focusing at varying distances, and not staring at one light for more than 10 seconds.
➢ False horizon: when the natural horizon is obscured, sloping clouds, bright stars, city lights, or shoreline lights over dark water can be mistaken for the horizon, leading the pilot to misalign the aircraft. Cross-check the flight instruments.

cards.question: How long does night (dark) adaptation take, and how can a pilot protect it?
cards.answer:
The cones adapt quickly, but the rods take up to about 30 minutes to fully adapt to darkness. Exposure to a bright light (landing lights, searchlights, flares) for 1 second or more impairs night vision, and the adaptation process must be repeated. Anti-collision strobes are too brief to impair it.

➢ Allow about 30 minutes in low light before relying on night vision
➢ If safe, close one eye when a bright light exposure begins to preserve that eye's adaptation
➢ Use off-center viewing (look about 10° away from an object) and scan in short stops of no more than 2-3 seconds

cards.question: What are the phases of a spin, and what is the general spin recovery procedure?
cards.answer:
Phases: entry, incipient, developed, recovery.

Recovery (always use the AFM/POH procedure first; otherwise):
1. Power to idle
2. Ailerons neutral
3. Full opposite rudder, held until rotation stops
4. Brisk, positive forward elevator (forward of neutral) to break the stall - immediately after rudder
5. Neutralize rudder when rotation stops
6. Smoothly return to level flight, avoiding a secondary stall and G/airspeed limits

Memory aid: PARE (Power, Ailerons, Rudder, Elevator). Use the turn indicator, not the ball, to determine spin direction. The first turn of a spin may lose about 1,000 ft; each additional turn about half that.

cards.question: What should a pilot do if the engine fails at night in a single-engine airplane?
cards.answer:
➢ Maintain control; establish best glide configuration and airspeed; turn toward an airport or away from congested areas
➢ Troubleshoot (fuel selector, magnetos, primer) and attempt a restart if possible
➢ Declare the emergency to ATC or UNICOM (stay on your current frequency unless told otherwise)
➢ If the terrain is known and suitable, plan to land on an unlighted portion of the area; consider a site near public access
➢ Land into the wind
➢ Complete the before-landing checklist; turn on landing lights in time to see obstacles. Land at the slowest possible airspeed; with no lights or visual reference, hold a level-landing attitude until touchdown
➢ After landing, turn off all switches and evacuate

cards.question: What is the general procedure for an engine fire in flight?
cards.answer:
Unless the AFM/POH says otherwise:
➢ Shut off fuel: mixture to idle cutoff and fuel selector/shutoff valve OFF
➢ Leave the ignition ON to burn the fuel remaining in the lines
➢ Do not attempt to restart if the fire goes out
➢ An oil-fed fire (thick black smoke) may require stopping the propeller to stop the engine-driven oil pump
➢ Consider leaving the master ON unless the fire is electrical or a crash landing is imminent (keeps radios and transponder available)
➢ Use the emergency descent procedure and make a forced landing as soon as possible

The airplane may be structurally damaged; treat it as expendable.

cards.question: How should a pilot handle an electrical fire in flight?
cards.answer:
The first sign is usually the smell of burning insulation.
➢ Try to identify and isolate the faulty circuit (circuit breakers, instruments, avionics, lights)
➢ If it can't be isolated and conditions permit, turn OFF the battery master and alternator switches
➢ If electrical power is essential: master OFF, all electrical switches OFF, master back ON, then turn needed switches on one at a time, pausing to check for smoke or odor
➢ Land as soon as possible - burning material may continue to burn even with power off

cards.question: Steep Spiral (CA.V.B): What is the purpose and what are the ACS standards?
cards.answer:
Purpose: lose a lot of altitude rapidly while staying over a selected point (useful for an emergency landing). A gliding turn of constant radius around a ground reference.

ACS standards:
➢ At least three 360° turns, starting high enough to finish no lower than 1,500 ft AGL
➢ Bank not to exceed 60° at the steepest point; correct for wind to keep a constant radius (steepest bank downwind)
➢ Maintain the specified airspeed ±10 knots
➢ Roll out toward an object or specified heading ±10°

Tip: periodically clear the engine during the glide to avoid excessive cooling, plug fouling, or carb ice.
cards.ref: Commercial Pilot ACS CA.V.B; AFH Chapter 10

cards.question: Chandelle (CA.V.C): How is it flown, and what are the ACS standards?
cards.answer:
A maximum-performance 180° climbing turn ending wings-level, nose-high, just above stall speed.

➢ Enter at the manufacturer's recommended speed (often VA or VO), flaps and gear up
➢ First 90°: constant bank (about 30°), continuously increasing pitch, add power
➢ Second 90°: constant pitch, constant-rate rollout, wings level at the 180° point

ACS standards:
➢ No lower than 1,500 ft AGL
➢ Bank approximately 30°
➢ Complete rollout at the 180° point ±10°, just above stall speed, holding that airspeed momentarily without stalling
➢ Resume straight-and-level flight with minimum loss of altitude
cards.ref: Commercial Pilot ACS CA.V.C; AFH Chapter 10

cards.question: Lazy Eights (CA.V.D): How are they flown, and what are the ACS standards?
cards.answer:
Two symmetrical 180° turns in opposite directions, each with a climb (first 90°) and descent (second 90°). Control pressures change constantly.
➢ 45° point: maximum pitch-up, about 15° bank
➢ 90° point: maximum bank (about 30°), minimum airspeed, pitch passing through level
➢ 135° point: maximum pitch-down, about 15° bank
➢ 180° point: level flight at entry altitude and airspeed

ACS standards:
➢ No lower than 1,500 ft AGL; coordinated throughout
➢ Approximately 30° bank at the steepest point
➢ At each 180° point: altitude ±100 ft, airspeed ±10 knots, heading ±10° from entry
cards.ref: Commercial Pilot ACS CA.V.D; AFH Chapter 10

cards.question: Eights on Pylons (CA.V.E): How do you find pivotal altitude, and what are the ACS standards?
cards.answer:
Pivotal altitude (rule of thumb) = groundspeed² ÷ 11.3 (knots) or ÷ 15 (mph), plus the pylon elevation (MSL). It depends on groundspeed, not bank angle.

➢ Choose two pylons perpendicular to the wind, at the same elevation, allowing 3-5 seconds of straight flight between them
➢ Enter diagonally crosswind so the first turn is into the wind
➢ Reference line ahead of the pylon: climb. Behind the pylon: descend. Don't use rudder to hold the pylon

ACS standards:
➢ Determine approximate pivotal altitude and select suitable pylons
➢ Bank not to exceed 40°
➢ Keep the line-of-sight reference on the pylon with smooth corrections, avoiding slips and skids
cards.ref: Commercial Pilot ACS CA.V.E; AFH Chapter 7

cards.question: What is time of useful consciousness (TUC), and roughly how long is it at high altitudes?
cards.answer:
TUC is the time from loss of oxygen supply until a person can no longer take proper corrective action. Impairment may begin immediately.

Approximate TUC (AC 61-107B):
➢ 18,000 ft: 20-30 min
➢ 22,000 ft: 10 min
➢ 25,000 ft: 3-5 min
➢ 28,000 ft: 2.5-3 min
➢ 30,000 ft: 1-2 min
➢ 35,000 ft: 30 sec-1 min
➢ 40,000 ft: 15-20 sec
➢ 43,000 ft and above: 9-12 sec

A rapid decompression cuts TUC by about 50%. Physical activity, fatigue, smoking, and illness also reduce it. Use 100% oxygen immediately.

cards.question: Under Part 91, can an Electronic Flight Bag (EFB) replace paper charts and documents, and what are the conditions?
cards.answer:
Yes - no formal FAA approval is needed for Part 91 operators if:
➢ The EFB does not replace any system or equipment required by Part 91 (navigation, communication, surveillance)
➢ It displays information functionally equivalent to the paper it replaces
➢ The information is current and valid, as verified by the pilot
➢ Its use complies with 91.21 (no interference with required equipment)

In-flight use is the decision of the operator and PIC. Plan for failure (backup power or device) and secure the device during takeoff and landing.

cards.question: What does AC 91-73B recommend for single-pilot taxi operations?
cards.answer:
➢ Plan before moving: review NOTAMs/ATIS for closures, the airport diagram, and hot spots; brief the expected route, hold-short lines, and runway crossings
➢ Have the current airport diagram displayed during taxi
➢ Do heads-down tasks (programming GPS/FMS, checklists, performance data) only while stopped or taxiing straight with no complex intersections
➢ Maintain a sterile cockpit, but encourage others to speak up
➢ Never cross a hold-short line without an explicit clearance; scan the full runway and final approach before entering or crossing
➢ If unsure of position: stop, tell ATC, and request progressive taxi

cards.question: What factors increase the risk of a runway overrun on landing?
cards.answer:
➢ Unstabilized approach
➢ Excess airspeed: about 10% fast on final ≈ 20% more landing distance
➢ Excess height over the threshold: each 10 ft above 50 ft adds about 200 ft of landing distance
➢ Touching down beyond the intended point
➢ High airport elevation / density altitude (higher true and groundspeed)
➢ Higher landing weight: about 10% heavier ≈ 10% more landing distance
➢ Downhill slope: 1% down ≈ 10% more distance
➢ Delayed braking or deceleration devices
➢ Tailwind: about 21% more landing distance for the first 10 knots
➢ Wet or contaminated runways (reduced braking action)

Mitigation: fly a stabilized approach at the proper speed and touch down at the intended point - go around if you can't.

cards.question: What is Controlled Flight Into Terrain (CFIT), and how can a GA pilot reduce the risk?
cards.answer:
CFIT occurs when an airworthy aircraft, under the control of a qualified pilot, is flown into terrain, water, or obstacles with inadequate awareness of the impending collision. Per the AC, GA CFIT accounted for about 17% of GA fatalities, and more than half occurred in IMC.

Key points:
➢ Continued VFR flight into IMC ("scud running") is a leading cause - get complete weather and make go/no-go and diversion decisions early
➢ Most accidents happen in takeoff/initial climb and final approach/landing (~6% of flight time) - stay vigilant in those phases
➢ Low flying: wires, obstacles, glare, shadows, darkness, and density altitude are common factors
➢ Use terrain awareness tools (TAWS/GPS terrain) and respond immediately to warnings
➢ Plan thoroughly, use a decision model (DECIDE), and operate within the aircraft's limits

cards.question: What does AC 90-109A recommend when transitioning to an unfamiliar airplane?
cards.answer:
Pilot performance when transitioning to an unfamiliar airplane is a leading factor in fatal accidents.
➢ Get airplane-specific transition training (systems, normal, abnormal, and emergency procedures) from an instructor experienced in that make/model
➢ Study the AFM/POH and the airplane's handling and performance characteristics
➢ Build significant day VFR experience in the new airplane before night or IFR operations
➢ Subsequent owners of experimental airplanes should get specific training before flying them
